## [RSOD distills multiple telecom LoRA teachers into one deployable student adapter](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.27993) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces Routed Specialist On-Policy Distillation (RSOD), an end-to-end framework that builds source-grounded synthetic telecom data, trains six specialist LoRA teachers on a shared continued-pretrained backbone, and consolidates them into a single student adapter released as Llama-CalixCLM v1. On 2,850 held-out questions, the student scores 21.7112/25 micro, within 0.0529 points of the combined six-teacher system (21.7641/25) and far above the raw Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct baseline (12.8661/25). This work shows that multiple domain-specialist LoRA teachers can be consolidated into a single deployable adapter without meaningful performance loss, which matters for telecom operators that need one practical model covering routing, broadband, access technologies, and diagnostics. The numerically validated train-serve path also addresses auditability concerns in regulated telecom deployments. RSOD has the committed student generate each trajectory, the route-assigned teacher force the exact native token sequence, and teacher hidden states be reconstructed through the shared frozen output head, updating only the student LoRA. A reconstruction check showed mean absolute logit error of 7.26×10^-6 with 100% top-1 agreement, and the 2,000-step run on four RTX 6000 Ada GPUs produced 16,000 trajectories with zero version or token-ID mismatches.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 22, 04:00

**Background**: LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) is a parameter-efficient fine-tuning technique that freezes a model's pretrained weights and injects small trainable rank-decomposition matrices, making it cheap to train multiple task-specific adapters. Knowledge distillation transfers behavior from teacher models to a student model, and on-policy distillation has the student generate its own trajectories so it learns to correct its own errors. Telecom language models need both broad networking knowledge and specialist behavior across routing, broadband services, access technologies, and operational diagnostics, yet must be deployable as a single model.

## [Dancing Diffusion turns diffusion conditioning into a latent program](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28003) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Dancing Diffusion introduces a method that assigns each span of timesteps in a diffusion model's denoising trajectory a dedicated continuous condition block, effectively turning conditioning into a latent program. A compiler maps text features into this program, and a fixed pretrained generator (SANA) executes the blocks over successive sampling intervals, allowing the trajectory to be redirected while preserving executed history. This work enables fine-grained control over the denoising trajectory, allowing operations to be addressed individually rather than applying a single instruction to every step. It could improve image editing by preserving content fixed by earlier operations and lays a foundation for structured intermediate computation in diffusion models. On SANA, reusing an executed prefix preserves markedly more of the scene than regenerating from noise at a similar edit strength, and learned conditions preserve more background than native prompt switching from the same saved state. However, later branches weaken the edit, leaving semantic control over individual operations limited.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 22, 04:00

**Background**: Diffusion models generate images by iteratively denoising a noisy sample over many timesteps, but typically condition every step on the same text prompt, so the trajectory cannot be controlled at the level of individual operations. SANA is an efficient high-resolution text-to-image diffusion transformer developed by NVIDIA. Dancing Diffusion reformulates conditioning as a program of addressable blocks, where a compiler trained via visual feedback maps text features into continuous condition blocks executed by a pretrained generator.

Researchers present IECG, a weakly-supervised ECG foundation model that jointly performs diagnostic classification and abnormality localization without manual region annotations. It derives abnormality heatmap pseudo-labels from established clinical ECG knowledge and uses a KL-divergence loss to guide the model's CLS-token attention toward diagnostically relevant waveform regions. Lack of interpretability is a major barrier to clinical adoption of ECG machine learning, and IECG addresses this by grounding predictions in localized waveform evidence without sacrificing classification performance. This could accelerate trustworthy deployment of ECG foundation models in real clinical workflows. During pretraining, IECG is jointly optimized with clinically guided attention supervision, ECG-text contrastive alignment, and report captioning objectives, learning multimodal representations while producing localized evidence. Experiments show state-of-the-art abnormal region localization while maintaining strong classification performance.

## [InsightRAG Uses Author-Written Related Work to Improve Automatic Survey Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28085) ⭐️ 7.0/10

InsightRAG proposes using author-written Related Work sections as distributed human judgments to guide retrieval and taxonomy construction for automatic scientific survey generation. It introduces insight-guided retrieval that follows author-supported citation relations to reconstruct a verified research scope and aggregates these judgments under a minimum-conflict objective into a taxonomy that reflects recurring author perspectives. This approach addresses key limitations of existing survey generation systems, such as incomplete scope, weak taxonomies, and unreliable citations, by leveraging the community's own navigation of the literature. It could lead to more reliable and comprehensive automatic surveys, benefiting researchers who rely on them to keep up with rapid scientific growth. The system aggregates author judgments under a minimum-conflict objective to build a taxonomy that guides generation and bounds each section's evidence. Results on ten topics show gains in scope reconstruction, taxonomy quality, citation support, and reference reliability, though it is an early arXiv preprint without community discussion yet.

## [Semi-Analytical Inference Framework for Structural Causal Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28103) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper proposes a message passing scheme directly on Structural Causal Models (SCMs) using a common finite-dimensional function space with B-spline bases, enabling unified forward and backward inference for observational, interventional, and counterfactual reasoning. Forward propagation combines a numerical realization of the Law of the Unconscious Statistician (LOTUS) with spline projection to recover densities, while backward message passing handles conditioning. This framework offers a unified approach to causal inference that avoids transforming SCMs into alternative representations or relying on approximate inference with generative models, potentially improving accuracy and efficiency for observational, interventional, and counterfactual queries. It could impact fields relying on causal modeling, such as epidemiology and machine learning. Using tensor-product B-spline bases, the algorithm expresses inference through numerical quadrature and linear algebra without explicitly constructing conditional distributions. Experiments on randomly generated continuous SCMs show accurate approximation of Monte Carlo reference solutions and systematic improvement with increasing basis resolution.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 22, 04:00

**Background**: Structural Causal Models (SCMs) are a framework for representing causal mechanisms using structural equations and directed acyclic graphs, enabling reasoning about interventions and counterfactuals. Probabilistic inference in SCMs is challenging because it requires computing distributions over variables, often relying on approximations or transformations. B-splines are piecewise polynomial functions used as a basis for function approximation, and the Law of the Unconscious Statistician (LOTUS) is a theorem for computing expected values of functions of random variables.

## [S-Agent 2.0: Spatial Reasoning with a General Coding Agent](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28354) ⭐️ 7.0/10

S-Agent 2.0 equips an off-the-shelf general coding agent with a command-line perception toolkit and persistent scene memory, helping VLMs close the evidence loop in spatial reasoning. This work targets a real gap in agentic VLMs: tools often return correct evidence but the model fails to convert raw readings into usable conclusions. By wrapping a coding agent with a CLI perception toolkit and persistent memory, it offers a general, harness-agnostic approach that works across Codex and Claude Code, potentially advancing multimodal AI systems that must reason about 3D space. With the open backbone, S-Agent 2.0 reaches 66.5 on MMSI-Bench and 82.3 on ReVSI, ahead of the specialized SpatialClaw system (62.6 and 74.5) on the same backbone; with Gemini-3.8-Flash it reaches 74.1 and 90.5 versus SpatialClaw's 67.0 and 79.7. The authors note that tool gains shrink as the backbone grows more capable, but SpatialClaw's gains shrink far more on ReVSI (from +13.2 to +2.7) while S-Agent 2.0's stays at +9.6.

## [FALCA: Falsification-Aware RL for Long-Horizon Deep Search Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28361) ⭐️ 7.0/10

FALCA introduces a falsification-aware reinforcement learning framework that formulates deep search as a propose-falsify process, using a collaborative Searcher-Falsifier architecture where independent Falsifiers actively seek counterevidence and produce falsification reports. It combines SFT warmup on falsification trajectories with agentic RL using parallel rollouts and hierarchical credit assignment over research stages, state transitions, and actions. Long-horizon deep search agents often suffer from error amplification, where early mistakes anchor reasoning and lead to confirmation bias; FALCA directly targets this by training agents to actively falsify hypotheses, potentially improving reliability of LLM-based research agents on complex information-seeking tasks. Experiments on five search benchmarks show gains over backbone and harness ablations, suggesting the approach could inform future agentic RL designs for long-horizon reasoning. The framework uses parallel rollouts and hierarchical credit assignment across research stages, state transitions, and actions to strengthen the falsification loop, and experiments show reduced confirmation bias and error accumulation. As an arXiv preprint, it lacks peer review and community validation, and the abstract does not report specific performance numbers or comparisons to state-of-the-art baselines.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 22, 04:00

**Background**: Deep search agents are LLM-based systems that iteratively decompose complex questions, retrieve evidence from external sources, and maintain a research state to answer multi-constraint queries. Reinforcement learning for LLM agents typically assigns credit to actions based on final outcomes, but long-horizon tasks suffer from delayed and sparse rewards, making it hard to identify which steps caused success or failure. Hierarchical credit assignment addresses this by decomposing rewards across levels such as stages, state transitions, and actions. Falsification, the deliberate search for counterexamples, is a complementary strategy to verification that helps catch errors early.

## [RACE: RoPE-Aligned Attention Compression via Query-Key Activation Energies](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28385) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers propose RACE, a post-training method that compresses attention head dimensions by selecting complete rotary pairs based on joint query-key activation energy, enabling natively reduced-dimensional attention without runtime reconstruction. At 50% KV-cache retention and 256K context, RACE reduces total inference FLOPs by 47.8%, achieving 1.79x higher throughput, 43.2% lower time-to-first-token, and 28.1% lower GPU memory compared to an uncompressed model. This work addresses the KV-cache memory bottleneck in long-context LLM inference by eliminating the reconstruction overhead common in prior compression methods, potentially enabling more efficient deployment of large models. It offers a theoretically grounded, kernel-free approach that could be integrated into existing inference pipelines without specialized hardware support. RACE restricts compression to coordinate selection and theoretically proves that RoPE compatibility holds if and only if complete rotary pairs are retained; the selection criterion minimizes a calibration-dependent upper bound on post-RoPE query-key product approximation error. The reductions are folded into model weights, requiring no runtime reconstruction or specialized kernels, and RACE outperforms structured pruning while remaining competitive with reconstruction-based methods across three model families.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 22, 04:00

**Background**: Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE) is a widely used technique that encodes positional information by rotating query and key vectors, enabling relative position awareness and long-context scaling in modern LLMs. KV-cache stores key and value tensors for previously processed tokens to avoid recomputation during autoregressive decoding, but its memory grows linearly with context length, becoming a major bottleneck for long-context inference. Prior KV-cache compression methods often reconstruct full-dimensional representations at inference time, adding significant decoding FLOPs overhead.

## [Stratified Sparse Attention Narrows the Sparse-to-Dense Gap at Extreme Sparsity](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28441) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduced Stratified Sparse Attention (SSA), a unified framework that combines deterministic retrieval of high-scoring tokens with score-guided sampling of the residual attention mass, correcting for inclusion probabilities. On RULER-HARD with Ministral-3-8B at 50× attention sparsity, SSA improved accuracy from 81.8% to 84.2% at 32K context and from 63.8% to 69.3% at 128K, recovering 94% and 85% of dense-attention performance respectively. Long-context LLM inference is increasingly bottlenecked by the growing KV cache, and SSA shows that accuracy gains at aggressive sparsity can translate into real speedups—up to 2.96× decode speedup over FlashInfer at 1M context with optimized CUDA kernels. This could make million-token context windows more practical for deployment. SSA generalizes top-k, top-p, and hybrid top-k+sampling as special cases, and was evaluated across RULER, LongBench, LOFT, and AIME on five models ranging from 3B to 27B parameters. The method samples the residual using proxy attention scores and corrects for inclusion probabilities, recovering attention mass beyond the retrieval set.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 22, 04:00

**Background**: In transformer-based LLMs, attention over long contexts requires storing key-value (KV) pairs for all previous tokens, and this KV cache grows linearly with context length, becoming a major memory and compute bottleneck during inference. Sparse attention mitigates this by attending to only a subset of the cache, but existing approaches face a trade-off: deterministic top-k retrieval captures high-scoring tokens yet discards residual attention mass, while sampling improves coverage at the cost of higher variance. Hybrid methods combining top-k with uniform sampling still lag behind dense attention at aggressive sparsity levels.

A new arXiv paper (2610.28479) argues that information decomposition provides a unifying formal framework to operationalize and compare claims of synergy and emergence in AI systems. It proposes a falsifiable criterion: a system's behavior is emergent only if it carries synergistic information about task-relevant outcomes. This work addresses a significant conceptual gap by giving researchers a precise, testable way to evaluate emergence claims, which are often informal and incomparable. It could impact how AI systems—from attention heads to multi-agent teams and human-AI collaborations—are analyzed and compared across scales. ## [DecisionPivot: A Diagnostic Benchmark for LLM Decision Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28522) ⭐️ 7.0/10

DecisionPivot introduces a diagnostic benchmark of 48 tasks and 40,033 items across seven decision roles, including a core track of 7,800 items from 13 generated task families organized into contrast groups with solver-verified answers. Evaluating 40 decision models and 14 general models, it reveals large gaps hidden by aggregate scores—for example, two 27B models only 2.6 points apart on the reference track achieve contrast-group accuracies of 70.1% and 44.2%. This benchmark addresses a real gap in LLM evaluation by moving beyond item accuracy to measure contrast-group accuracy, probability ordering, calibration, and selective coverage, which are critical for decision models used in routing, guardrails, and output verification. It could help practitioners select models that are not just accurate on average but reliably calibrated and consistent under controlled variations. The benchmark includes a complementary reference track of 32,233 items from 35 public test sets with original metrics, and on a 1,296-item subset, GLM-5.3 achieves 93.5% contrast-group accuracy at a higher reasoning setting versus 81.5% at its lowest effort. Notably, across 2,400 binary contrast pairs, Perplexity Decider correctly ranks the positive member above the negative in 92.3% of pairs but answers both correctly in only 74.1%, exposing a gap between probability ordering and decision correctness.

**Background**: Decision models in LLM systems are components that make discrete choices such as routing queries, enforcing guardrails, or verifying outputs, and they are increasingly evaluated separately from general-purpose models. Contrast groups pair minimally different inputs to test whether a model responds to the pivotal detail rather than superficial cues.

## [2-bit PTQ: Vector Codebooks and Joint Data Selection Key](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28537) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.28537) systematically studies post-training quantization (PTQ) below 4 bits across six dense and mixture-of-experts models (3.8B to 32B parameters), showing that at 2 bits the quantization representation—especially vector codebooks—is the dominant factor, and that calibration and recovery data must be jointly selected to recover accuracy. This work provides practical guidance for extreme compression, showing that a vector codebook representation with a small task-aligned calibration mixture and a cheap codebook-only recovery stage can retain 89–97% of full-precision QA accuracy at about 2.3 effective bits per weight, using 1.4–30× less compute than the strongest QAT baseline. The recipe uses about 2.3 effective bits per weight including codebooks, and most of the remaining accuracy loss is on generative tasks with model-dependent drop; at short recovery budgets, the best recovery data depends on the calibration data, so they must be chosen jointly.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 22, 04:00

**Background**: Post-training quantization (PTQ) compresses a trained model's weights using limited compute and data, and is near-lossless down to 4 bits, but at 2 bits scalar PTQ configurations fall to chance-level accuracy. Vector quantization is a classical technique that represents data using prototype vectors (codebooks), which can capture structure better than scalar quantization. Mixture-of-experts (MoE) models activate only a subset of parameters per token, making their quantization behavior different from dense models.

## [LLM-driven evolutionary search automates semantic index design for generative retrieval](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28568) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper introduces a framework that uses a locally served 31B open-weight LLM to mutate executable components of generative retrieval (GR), guided by a 1M-parameter proxy decoder that provides fast feedback. This is the first application of LLM-driven evolutionary program search to GR, addressing the long-standing limitation that SID components are hand-designed and cannot be optimized end-to-end with gradients. The proxy decoder shows strong rank correlation with the target 1B generator across 21 SID programs on NQ320K (Spearman ρ = 0.90), but a component study finds that proxy reliability depends on what is evolved: improvements transfer reliably for the semantic index but not for the generator's training objective or the full pipeline. ## [CoRAL: Hybrid Diffusion-Autoregressive Framework for Efficient Multimodal Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28584) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces CoRAL (Collaborative Reasoning Asymmetric Learning), a hybrid framework that combines a diffusion language model (DLM) planner with an autoregressive model (ARM) executor to overcome the sequentiality bottleneck in reasoning. The DLM planner generates K diverse reasoning trajectories in parallel, while the ARM executor selects the best plan and synthesizes the final answer, trained with a novel Reward-Guided Denoising for CoT (RDC) method. This work addresses a fundamental limitation of autoregressive models—their sequential token-by-token generation—by leveraging diffusion models for parallel reasoning, potentially enabling faster and more efficient multimodal reasoning. If successful, such hybrid architectures could influence the design of future vision-language models and reasoning systems. The framework uses an Asymmetric Planner-Executor (APE) architecture where the DLM planner generates multiple reasoning trajectories in parallel and the ARM executor selects and refines the final answer. Training involves Reward-Guided Denoising for CoT (RDC), which integrates outcome-based rewards into the diffusion process to steer the planner toward goal-directed reasoning.

**Background**: Autoregressive models (ARMs) generate text one token at a time, which can be slow and may suffer from error accumulation in long reasoning chains. Diffusion language models (DLMs) instead generate text by iteratively denoising a noisy sequence, allowing parallel generation but often lacking semantic coherence. CoRAL aims to combine the strengths of both paradigms.

A new arXiv paper introduces RTLRepairDataset (5,784 broken-fixed training pairs), RTLRepairBench (459 held-out cases with 374 syntactic and 85 behavioral mutations), and an evaluation harness supporting simulation and formal equivalence. Using this infrastructure, the authors identify two measurement confounds: simulation and formal scoring can give opposite signs for the effect of providing a specification, and the specification-only minus specification-conditioned recovery estimate ranges from -8.5 to +18.3 percentage points across six models. The paper proposes evaluation controls—reporting initialization, reset, first-cycle, and unknown-value semantics, disclosing oracle coverage, and including a specification-only baseline—that could improve rigor in LLM-for-EDA benchmarking. Reset-aware rescoring attributes almost all of the simulation-formal disagreement to reset and first-cycle comparison semantics, and the authors release the benchmark, training set, construction code, sanitized aggregate evidence, and reproduction materials on GitHub.

## [Adaptive Multi-Token Prediction Dynamically Tunes Speculation Horizon](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28619) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces Adaptive Multi-Token Prediction (AMTP), an online control method that dynamically selects the speculation horizon for multi-token prediction to balance acceleration and wasted compute, without retraining the model. It uses verification feedback to learn acceptance survival and picks the horizon with the highest expected tokens per second before each round. This work addresses a key inefficiency in multi-token prediction and speculative decoding: a fixed horizon can waste compute when drafts are rejected. By adaptively choosing the horizon per context, AMTP can improve inference throughput without changing the model or verifier, potentially benefiting any deployment using MTP heads or draft models. AMTP is a lightweight controller that leaves the exact verifier unchanged and learns from every verification pass; theoretically, its prediction error translates into throughput regret that is sublinear with online gradient descent. Evaluated on five draft-target pairings (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct with Medusa heads, Meta's MTP models, and Qwen3-4B-Inst-2507-MTP) on AIME 2025 and GSM8K, it decodes up to 4.1x faster than standard decoding and matches or outperforms the fixed window in 8 of 10 settings, with throughput gains up to 10%.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 22, 04:00

**Background**: Multi-token prediction (MTP) trains a language model to predict several future tokens at once using multiple output heads, which can speed up decoding by drafting multiple tokens and verifying them in a single target-model pass. Speculative decoding similarly uses a draft model to propose tokens that a larger target model verifies, accepting a prefix of drafts that match the target's distribution. The efficiency of both depends on the acceptance rate and draft length, but MTP must fix the horizon before drafting because all heads fire in the same forward pass, unlike autoregressive drafting where stopping can be decided token by token.

## [GRaSP: Latency-Aware Re-Scoring for Geo-Distributed RAG](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.26938) ⭐️ 7.0/10

GRaSP introduces a drop-in re-scoring layer for geo-distributed RAG that decays relevance by latency and adds an optional cost penalty under a cardinality budget and per-region caps, with no retraining. The authors prove the base formulation is a linear objective over a partition matroid solvable optimally by an O(N log N) greedy algorithm, and on a five-node CloudLab testbed emulating a four-region WAN over the Natural Questions corpus they cut P90 fetch latency by 41% while retaining 78% of relevance-only recall. As RAG pipelines spread across cloud and edge regions, wide-area latency, cross-region egress cost, and data-residency rules increasingly compete with retrieval quality, and conventional similarity-only ranking ignores where content lives. The benefit is placement-dependent: under uniform placement GRaSP cuts fetch latency at negligible quality cost, while under topical (residency-like) placement it traces a recall-latency Pareto frontier that dominates relevance-only, nearest-k, and a latency-budgeted baseline. Hardness enters only under an additive egress budget, and end-to-end question answering shows a 43% context-fetch latency reduction while staying within 0.062 absolute EM of relevance-only retrieval, with findings generalizing across four public BEIR benchmarks.

## [3D-MoE: Complementarity-Guided Co-Design for MoE Decode on 3D-Stacked NMP](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.26991) ⭐️ 7.0/10

3D-MoE introduces a hardware-software co-design that exploits 'expert complementarity'—offsetting expert-load fluctuations across decode steps—to balance MoE inference on 3D-stacked near-memory processing (NMP). It combines offline complementarity-guided grouping, a lightweight Collaborative Memory-Network (CMN) for residual hotspots, and cost-aware online remapping, achieving an average 4.63× MoE-layer speedup over expert parallelism and 1.58×–1.86× end-to-end throughput improvement over the strongest NMP baselines with only 2.11% additional logic-die area. MoE decode is highly memory-bound with skewed, time-varying expert loads, and 3D-stacked NMP offers the needed bandwidth but struggles with load balancing due to its tiled organization. This work resolves the locality-balance conflict, potentially enabling more efficient LLM inference on emerging near-memory computing architectures and influencing future hardware-software co-design for AI systems. The approach uses offline one-time complementarity-guided grouping and locality-aware mapping for coarse-grained inter-group balance, while the CMN streams each hot expert's weight tiles once from its host DRAM channel to helper cores over a reconfigured local broadcast path. Cost-aware online remapping handles workload drift, and the overhead is only 2.11% additional logic-die area.

## [Scaffolds Compute NL-Complete Closures That Distilled Students Cannot Represent](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.27157) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv preprint (2610.27157) proves that inference-time harnesses can compute an NL-complete closure of their per-call primitive even when that primitive is a trivial AC0 lookup, and that no fixed-depth forward pass can represent this under the widely believed conjecture that NL is not contained in TC0. Empirically, the authors show that distilled students fail to match harness performance, and that enlarging the student, simplifying the task, or lengthening chain-of-thought can close the gap. This work provides a fundamental representational explanation for why distillation fails to internalize the benefits of inference-time scaffolding, suggesting that simply training a same-class student on harness traces cannot transfer the harness's computational power into the weights. It has implications for how practitioners should think about combining inference-time computation with model training and for the limits of current distillation approaches. The theoretical result hinges on the conjecture that NL ⊄ TC0, which is widely believed but unproven; the gap is shown to reappear in an agentic harness on competition math, and the authors verify empirically that increasing the student's representational capacity relative to the task (e.g., by enlarging the model, making the task easier, or lengthening chain-of-thought) is necessary to close the gap.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 22, 04:00

**Background**: Inference-time harnesses (or scaffolds) are external procedures that call a language model many times and keep state across calls, often improving performance without changing model weights. Computational complexity classes such as AC0 (constant-depth, polynomial-size circuits), NL (nondeterministic logarithmic space), and TC0 (constant-depth threshold circuits) formalize what different computational models can express. Distillation attempts to train a smaller or same-class student model to mimic a teacher's behavior, but this paper shows a fundamental representational barrier when the teacher is a harness.

## [Language Models Underperform on Composed Tasks Due to Implicit Thinking Budget](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.27190) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.27190) shows that language models make substantially more errors when multiple tasks are composed into a single prompt, even when each task is solved reliably in isolation. The authors attribute this to an implicit thinking budget: under composition, models allocate fewer tokens per task, and tasks requiring longer solution traces become more fragile. This identifies a practically important failure mode for anyone building multi-task prompts, since performance degradation cannot be explained by independent error accumulation alone. The finding suggests that grouping tasks by fragility can reduce token usage by 43% while preserving accuracy, offering a path to more efficient prompting. The study covers both open-weight models and the frontier model Claude Opus 5, and the degradation persists even when the full sequence remains well within the context window. In isolation, non-fragile tasks receive more reasoning than needed and waste compute, which the authors exploit by grouping tasks according to fragility.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 22, 04:00

**Background**: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to handle multiple tasks within a single prompt, requiring them to solve each task and integrate answers coherently. Open-weight models are those whose parameters are publicly available for inspection and fine-tuning, while thinking budget refers to the number of tokens a model spends on internal reasoning before answering. The context window is the maximum number of tokens a model can process at once, and prior work has explored controlling reasoning length via budget guidance.

The benchmark includes six localized websites instantiated in five languages, yielding 3,000 task instances, and evaluates three closed-source and five open-source models. Post-training on a small subset of LoWAgent traces significantly improves low-resource language performance, demonstrating the benchmark's utility for targeted fine-tuning.

## [Profile-DP: Local Differential Privacy for Personalized LLM Profile Release](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.27213) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Profile-DP introduces a policy-aware local differential privacy framework and two finite-domain mechanisms, DP-SLOT and DP-BLOCK, to bound the release of user-withheld profile facts during personalized LLM inference. On the PEEP benchmark, DP-BLOCK leads the utility composite among DP methods at all 13 structured budgets and is closest to the ideal privacy-utility point in 18 of 26 format-budget settings. Personalized LLMs increasingly condition responses on rich user profiles, which exposes sensitive facts and explicit sharing preferences; Profile-DP provides formal privacy guarantees that decouple from downstream model behavior. This makes policy-aware profile release a practical foundation for studying the privacy-personalization trade-off, relevant to privacy and ML researchers building user-facing LLM systems. DP-SLOT independently perturbs protected attributes, while DP-BLOCK uses public semantic decisions to coordinate release and jointly sample related attributes, connected by a positive public compatibility prior that preserves a profile-level privacy bound. Direct measurements show complementary strengths: DP-BLOCK discloses less, whereas DP-SLOT retains more authorized facts.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 22, 04:00

**Background**: Local differential privacy (LDP) is a privacy model in which each user perturbs their data on their own device before sending it to an untrusted server, so the server only receives differentially private data. Differential privacy is a mathematically rigorous framework that uses randomized mechanisms to release statistical information while protecting individual data subjects. Profile-conditioned inference pairs a public request with user-specific facts, a growing paradigm in personalized LLMs that raises concerns about exposing the profile itself.

## [AutoRedClaw: Automated Red-Teaming for Persistent Claw-Style Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.27244) ⭐️ 7.0/10

AutoRedClaw is an automated red-teaming framework that generates end-to-end attacks and the environments needed to execute them, targeting persistent, personalized claw-style agents like OpenClaw. It achieves an effective attack rate above 30% at less than $0.10 per successful sample and releases RedClaw-Bench, a 330-case benchmark that yields substantially higher attack success rates than AgentDojo, AgentDyn, and DTap. This work addresses a critical security gap: persistent agents that reload poisoned configuration files, memory, and skills across sessions create threats that manual testing cannot scale to cover. By automating both attack generation and environment construction, AutoRedClaw enables scalable, up-to-date security evaluation for the growing class of personalized agent systems, with most tested agent harnesses exceeding 50% attack success rate. AutoRedClaw combines a strict quality-checking protocol with execution-based validation to ensure correctness, realism, and effectiveness of generated samples, and uses task-driven environment construction to keep costs low. It organizes generation along risk categories, attack strategies, attack stages, and attack surfaces, with experience-guided exploration steering toward under-explored regions; across seven harnesses and four frontier models, most agent systems exceed 50% ASR.

**Background**: Claw-style agents such as OpenClaw are persistent, personalized assistants that maintain configuration files like AGENTS.md, long-term memory, and reusable skills, which are repeatedly reloaded into the agent's context. Red-teaming is the practice of adversarially probing AI systems to find vulnerabilities before deployment, but existing evaluation systems rely heavily on manually constructed test cases and environments that limit scale and coverage and quickly become outdated. The paper introduces an iterative prompt-editing procedure that uses an LLM editor and judge to adapt source-grounded seed prompts to expose model-specific hallucinations. Experiments across 500 seeds, seven datasets, and ten topics show that editing substantially increases judge-rated hallucination severity, with retained responses falling in the strong-hallucination bin in 77.2% of extrinsic and 74.2% of intrinsic hallucination runs. This work addresses a key limitation of current hallucination benchmarks: similar average scores can mask model-specific failure modes. By generating target-aware stress tests, it enables more diagnostic evaluation of LLM safety and reliability, which is important for both open-weight and closed-source model deployment. Later editing rounds account for more than half of the mean score increase, and among 219 prompts passing model-assisted source-validity checks, 89 elicit unsupported claims. Across five models, 200 curated prompts yield similar average severity scores, but pairwise Spearman correlations between prompt-level scores are only ρ=0.0387 to 0.1897, indicating low cross-model consistency at the prompt level.

## [VPFlow: Value-Predictive Planning with Imperfect World Models for Offline Goal Reaching](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.27280) ⭐️ 7.0/10

VPFlow introduces a method that trains latent world models to predict goal-reaching value instead of future states, using a closed-form Monte Carlo return as the sole supervision signal. It pairs these value-predictive world models with a one-step flow policy and plans in the noise space via evolutionary search, outperforming model-free baselines by at least 30.3 and 10.1 percentage points on 30 state and pixel OGBench datasets, respectively. This work challenges the prevailing assumption in model-based reinforcement learning that accurate next-state prediction is necessary for effective planning, showing that value-predictive representations suffice and even outperform state-predictive ones. It could simplify world model training and improve offline goal-conditioned planning, impacting areas like robot learning from suboptimal demonstrations and zero-shot goal adaptation. Despite having latent prediction error orders of magnitude larger than state prediction, VPFlow achieves higher success rates, and minimizing this error actually lowers performance, demonstrating that value-predictive representations, not exact state prediction, are what offline planning requires. The method also reduces out-of-distribution queries common in action-space planning by planning in the noise space of a one-step flow policy.

**Background**: Offline goal-conditioned reinforcement learning aims to learn policies that reach any goal from any state using only a fixed dataset, without dense rewards. Temporal-difference (TD) bootstrapping is a common technique for learning value functions by updating estimates based on other estimates, but it can be unstable; VPFlow replaces it with a closed-form Monte Carlo return for goal reaching.

A new arXiv paper (2610.27301) evaluates context compaction methods on later questions across four annotated corpora and finds that selecting sentences for the current question does not beat random sentence deletion on subsequent questions, whereas question-agnostic word-level compression with LLMLingua-2 does, beating random deletion by 12.5 points on later MultiRC questions. This counterintuitive result challenges the common assumption that question-aware compaction is universally beneficial, and has direct implications for LLM agent design where compacted context must serve multiple future queries rather than just the current one. On MultiRC, keeping sentences judged necessary by gpt-6-luna raises current-question accuracy by 11.4 points at 25% of tokens, but the ranking reverses on Evidence Inference and τ-bench trajectories where exact identifiers matter; on FEVER, label accuracy can overstate what the kept text actually supports, and LLMLingua-2's 21.0-point gain is not shown to rest on the kept text.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 22, 04:00

**Background**: LLM agents often compress their context to fit token budgets, typically by selecting sentences relevant to the current question. LLMLingua-2 is a Microsoft Research prompt compression method that uses data distillation from GPT-4 to perform task-agnostic word-level compression, removing non-essential tokens without regard to the specific query. MultiRC is a multi-sentence reading comprehension dataset where questions require combining evidence from multiple sentences, making it suitable for testing whether compaction preserves evidence needed for later questions.

## [New Metric Exposes Vulnerability Monoculture in Foundation Model Pools](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.27353) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces Systemic Adversarial Robustness (SAR), a metric that quantifies shared vulnerabilities across a pool of models by measuring the attack diversity needed to compromise it. SAR interpolates between single-attack transferability and independent per-model robustness, with small values indicating a vulnerability monoculture where few attacks can cause widespread failure. This work highlights a critical but underexplored risk: as foundation models share common training pipelines and data, a single attack could catastrophically compromise an entire ecosystem. It provides a measurable target for holistic adversarial evaluation of model populations, affecting AI safety and security practices. SAR is formulated as a partial set-cover problem with provable approximation guarantees, enabling scalable algorithms. Empirically, model pools distilled from DeepSeek-R1 and Claude Opus 4.6 show lower systemic robustness than their parent pools, revealing a potential systemic cost of frontier-model distillation.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 22, 04:00

**Background**: Adversarial robustness typically measures how well a single model resists crafted inputs, and attack transferability describes how attacks designed for one model also fool others. Knowledge distillation compresses large models into smaller ones by training a student to mimic a teacher, often sharing vulnerabilities. This paper argues that shared algorithmic choices across models create a 'vulnerability monoculture' where failures are highly correlated.

## [LiBRA uses logit fingerprints for Byzantine-robust client selection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.27357) ⭐️ 7.0/10

LiBRA proposes comparing clients via class-conditional logit fingerprints of pseudo-patterns instead of parameter vectors, enabling Byzantine-robust client selection compatible with secure aggregation and heterogeneous architectures. It instantiates variants of Krum, Multi-Krum and Bulyan that change only the dissimilarity score, and on Fashion-MNIST and CIFAR-10 with three architectures and four attacks under i.i.d. partitions, each variant holds every attack its parent holds. This approach addresses a key limitation of existing Byzantine-robust aggregation rules, which require access to individual client updates and thus conflict with secure aggregation, and are restricted to clients sharing an architecture. By enabling robust client selection without reading client parameters, LiBRA could make federated learning more practical in privacy-sensitive and cross-device settings. The fingerprint consists of C^2 values for C classes, computed from each client's model response to pseudo-patterns optimized against it, and the trust decision reads no client parameter and compares up to 49,090 times fewer values. On identical client updates under a backdoor attack, the fingerprint ranks malicious clients within 0.006 AUC of the full parameter vector, at the cost of one pattern optimization per client per round; evaluation is limited to two datasets and i.i.d. partitions.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 22, 04:00

**Background**: Federated learning trains a shared model across many clients without centralizing their data, but malicious clients can send corrupted updates (Byzantine attacks). Robust aggregation rules like Krum, Multi-Krum and Bulyan defend by comparing clients' parameter vectors and filtering outliers, yet this requires seeing individual updates, which undermines secure aggregation—a cryptographic technique that keeps updates hidden—and only works when all clients share the same model architecture.

## [Predictive Closure: Set-Level View of JEPA Feature Selection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.27364) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper proposes a predictive closure characterization for JEPA, reformulating the training objective to show that feature selection depends on set-level properties of features rather than their individual predictability. Controlled experiments confirm that unpredictable features, such as a traffic light, can be retained when they help predict other features. This work addresses a key concern in JEPA that unpredictable but relationally useful features might be discarded, providing a theoretical foundation for understanding what JEPA encodes. It also offers practical implications for steering feature selection through auxiliary objectives or side information, which could improve representation learning in self-supervised settings. The characterization agrees with earlier predictability-based views when features evolve independently but makes new predictions when they are correlated, showing that steering one feature can indirectly affect the representation of another. The authors include Yoav Goldberg, and the work is a theoretical contribution with controlled experiments rather than large-scale empirical validation.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 22, 04:00

**Background**: JEPA (Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture) is a self-supervised learning framework that trains an encoder and a predictor to minimize the error in predicting the representation of the next observation, rather than reconstructing raw pixels or tokens. Because both current and next representations are learned, it is unclear which features the model will include. Earlier work characterized selected features by their individual predictability, raising concerns that unpredictable features would be omitted.

## [NR-SAE aligns sparse autoencoders with MoE router decisions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.27421) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces NR-SAE, which gives each routed expert in a Mixture-of-Experts model a small dictionary and opens only those selected by the frozen router. On Gemma 4 26B-A4B at block 15, after 10M C4 tokens and three seeds, it explains 0.518 of the variance in router-weighted expert outputs, outperforming three matched controls (0.481, 0.458, 0.387). This work suggests that MoE routing decisions already encode useful sparsity structure that a dictionary would otherwise have to learn, potentially simplifying interpretability for MoE models. It offers a new direction for mechanistic interpretability research on large sparse models. Part of the advantage is architectural: each expert writes into a subspace of at most a quarter of the model width, so naming the expert names the subspace, though the authors have not measured how much this explains. A transcoder variant also leads controls (0.432 vs. 0.347, 0.371, 0.118), but the implementation did not train faster, and semantic interpretability, downstream loss, and causal faithfulness remain untested.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 22, 04:00

**Background**: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are a common tool in mechanistic interpretability that decompose model activations into sparse, potentially interpretable features. Mixture-of-experts (MoE) models use a router to select a small subset of experts for each token, creating a sparse computation pattern. Transcoders are an alternative to SAEs that map activations between layers and have been shown to produce more interpretable features in some settings.

## [MLIPS shares sparse attention indexer pools across layers for faster LLM inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.27438) ⭐️ 7.0/10

MLIPS (Multi-Layer Indexer Pool Sharing) is a training-free method that lets a producer layer publish a top-M candidate pool larger than the attention budget K, from which subsequent consumer layers select their own top-K, avoiding a full-prefix scan at every layer. Implemented in vLLM for DeepSeek-V4-Flash with layerwise sharing, persistent decode reuse, and a coarse producer, it achieves 1.14–1.40x speedups and 14.8–27.4% lower GPU energy across four long-context suites, with accuracy changes of -1.49 to +0.29 percentage points in single runs. Sparse attention is a key enabler of long-context LLM serving, but the indexer's top-K search can become a latency bottleneck when repeated at every layer. MLIPS shows that much of this search is redundant across layers, offering a practical, training-free optimization that can be plugged into existing serving stacks like vLLM to reduce cost and energy without retraining models. The speedups and energy savings come with modest accuracy changes in single runs, but more extensive sharing exposes task-dependent quality losses, and the exploratory Top-G bounded pool construction for prefill remains undeployed with its accuracy and serving benefits still open. The method retains each consumer's own scoring and selection, so it is not simply reusing the producer's final top-K.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 22, 04:00

**Background**: Sparse attention reduces the number of keys each query attends to, but finding the relevant keys typically requires an indexer that scores all previous tokens and selects the top-K at every layer. In long-context serving, this per-layer full-prefix scan adds overhead, especially during decoding where it runs for each query token. vLLM is a popular LLM serving engine that uses PagedAttention and continuous batching to optimize KV cache memory and throughput, and DeepSeek-V4-Flash is a sparse mixture-of-experts model with 13B active parameters that uses DeepSeek Sparse Attention.

## [Learnable Graph Positional Encodings Scale Language Model Graph Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.27439) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper proposes augmenting language reasoning models with learnable, permutation-equivariant graph positional encodings computed by a GNN followed by a Graph Transformer, which modulate attention logits and are fused into hidden states. This eliminates serialized adjacency descriptions, reducing context length from O(E) to O(N), and the model is jointly fine-tuned with LoRA adapters using optimal solutions from graph-theoretic solvers. This approach addresses a key scalability bottleneck in graph reasoning for language models, enabling them to handle graphs up to 1,000 nodes with improved size generalization and fewer output tokens. It could impact AI for combinatorial optimization, network analysis, and other domains where large graphs are common. The model is trained on small graphs but generalizes to larger ones, remains robust to node relabelings, and preserves performance on small graphs; the joint fine-tuning of the positional encoder and LoRA adapters is computationally efficient.

**Background**: Language reasoning models typically solve graph tasks by serializing the graph's edges into text, which grows with the number of edges and limits problem size. Graph positional encodings are vectors that capture a node's structural role, and permutation equivariance ensures that reordering nodes does not change the model's output. LoRA is a parameter-efficient fine-tuning method that adapts large models by adding low-rank matrices.

## [VB-EGE: Adaptive Sampling for Pareto Frontier Identification in Multi-Objective LLM Arenas](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.27447) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces Vector-Borda Empirical-Gap Elimination (VB-EGE), a fixed-confidence adaptive sampling algorithm that efficiently identifies the Pareto frontier of LLMs in multi-objective arena-style evaluations. It provides theoretical guarantees, including an instance-dependent upper bound on sample complexity and a minimax-optimal lower bound up to logarithmic factors, and demonstrates empirical effectiveness on three real-world Arena datasets. This work addresses the high cost of human feedback in LLM evaluation by offering a principled alternative to scalar leaderboards, enabling reliable multi-objective comparisons with fewer pairwise judgments. It could significantly impact evaluation methodology by making arena-style assessments more efficient and statistically sound. VB-EGE operates under a multi-objective Bradley-Terry model and progressively eliminates models from an active set once sufficient statistical evidence certifies their Pareto status. The algorithm is evaluated through simulations and experiments on Arena, SearchArena, and VisionArena datasets, showing empirical effectiveness.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 22, 04:00

**Background**: In multi-objective optimization, the Pareto frontier is the set of solutions that are not dominated by any other solution, representing optimal trade-offs among competing objectives. LLM evaluation is inherently multi-objective, as models may perform differently across dimensions like math, code, and writing. Arena-style evaluations collect human pairwise preferences, which are costly, and the Bradley-Terry model is commonly used to estimate model strengths from such comparisons. Adaptive sampling algorithms like LUCB aim to identify top candidates with fixed confidence using as few samples as possible.

## [Projected Distillation Edits Failed Attempts for On-Policy Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.27467) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces projected distillation, a method that minimally edits a student model's failed attempts into correct targets to provide near-on-policy learning signals on hard problems. It uses contrastive updates to favor corrections over failed attempts and refreshes these corrections as the student evolves, and theoretically shows that learning regret scales linearly with edit size under minimal correction versus quadratically under full-answer replacement. This work addresses a key limitation of on-policy reinforcement learning and distillation: when all attempts fail on hard problems, there is no learning signal, and off-policy targets can erode existing capabilities. By enabling near-on-policy learning even when all student attempts fail, projected distillation could improve LLM post-training on challenging tasks while preserving retention, as demonstrated by its highest area under the specialization-retention frontier across two students and five domains. The method was evaluated on Qwen3-8B and OLMo-2-7B across five domains including math, code, science, and tool use, achieving the best specialization-retention frontier in 8 of 9 cells against GRPO and OPD, and 7 of 9 against SPOT and SODA. Ablations show that retention falls from 0.916 to 0.744 when minimal corrections are replaced by student-agnostic gold solutions, highlighting the importance of online corrections, the contrastive loss, and on-policyness.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 22, 04:00

**Background**: On-policy learning, where a model trains on its own generations, is central to LLM post-training because it limits distribution shift and helps preserve existing capabilities. On-policy distillation provides dense next-token supervision from a teacher on the student's own rollouts, but on hard problems, early mistakes in a rollout contaminate subsequent supervision. Off-policy targets from gold or teacher solutions can differ substantially from the student's generations and may cause forgetting, motivating methods that balance on-policyness with correct supervision.

## [EmbGA: Genetic Algorithm Recovers Hidden Concepts in Text-to-Image Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.27473) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces EmbGA, an embedding-space genetic algorithm that recovers visual concepts present in generated images but absent from their prompts. It outperforms six optimizers on two benchmarks, achieving the highest alignment with large exploration budgets and recovering the most grounded tokens on natural images while running much faster than language-model-guided search. This work enables auditing of implanted associations in text-to-image models, which is crucial for AI safety and transparency. It provides a practical tool to detect hidden biases or maliciously inserted concepts that ordinary prompts might trigger, affecting model developers, auditors, and users relying on these models. EmbGA operates in the token embedding space, using crossover to interpolate between parent embeddings and mutation to move embeddings toward random vocabulary embeddings, then projects offspring back to discrete tokens for scoring. It requires no gradient access to the scoring encoder and avoids the per-candidate inference cost of language-model-guided search.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 22, 04:00

**Background**: Text-to-image models can generate visual concepts not mentioned in their prompts, and recent research shows such associations can be intentionally implanted so that ordinary prompts trigger them. Auditing this behavior requires recovering the omitted description, but existing prompt optimizers are ill-suited: gradient-based methods need backward access to the scoring encoder, discrete evolutionary search treats unrelated tokens as equally close, and language-model-guided search is slow due to one inference call per candidate. EmbGA addresses these limitations by applying genetic operators in the continuous embedding space while ensuring every evaluated candidate is a valid token sequence.

## [OBU: SVD-based unlearning removes dual-use risks without collateral damage](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.27490) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces Orthogonal Boundary Unlearning (OBU), a framework that uses singular value decomposition (SVD) on calibration activations to identify a domain-matched capability subspace and restricts parameter updates to its orthogonal null space. Two implementations are presented: Projected LoRA (iterative fine-tuning with orthogonal constraints) and Closed-Form Weight Surgery (single-step analytical weight editing without training). This addresses a critical challenge in AI safety: removing hazardous dual-use capabilities (e.g., cyberwarfare, pathogen enhancement) from LLMs without degrading legitimate scientific knowledge, a problem known as concept bleeding. If validated, OBU could enable safer deployment of open-weight models while preserving defensive utility. OBU was evaluated on four open-weight models (Gemma-3-4B, Qwen3.5-4B, SmolLM3-3B, Granite-4.2-3B), showing strong dual-use concept separation, mitigation of in-context priming attacks, and durable resistance to adversarial relearning without degrading benign domain competence. The method guarantees zero parameter perturbation along the calibration subspace for benign representations.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 22, 04:00

**Background**: Machine unlearning aims to remove specific information or capabilities from trained models without full retraining. In dual-use domains like cybersecurity and biotech, benign and malicious knowledge share vocabulary and internal representations, so standard unlearning often causes concept bleeding—degrading legitimate capabilities. SVD is a matrix factorization that reveals the principal directions of variance in data, and its null space can be used to constrain updates to avoid affecting certain representations.

## [RSD: Self-Evolving Agents Learn from Privileged Retrospective Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.27495) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces Retrospective Self-Distillation (RSD), a multi-round framework where the same model acts as both student and teacher, using privileged retrospective context—cross-task precedents, turn-level reflection, and future hindsight—to generate dense supervision from on-policy trajectories without ground-truth rewards. Across ALFWorld, ScienceWorld, and SearchQA with Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-14B, RSD improves performance by up to 59.7% relative to the base model, and frontier-guided context-policy evolution adds up to a further 44.7% relative improvement. This work shows that naturally accumulated experience can be converted into persistent model capability without ground-truth trajectories or verifier-derived rewards, which is significant for deploying self-improving LLM agents in open-ended environments where such supervision is unavailable. It also introduces a frontier-guided mechanism for co-evolving the context policy, pointing toward scalable self-evolution pipelines. The teacher re-scores the student's realized actions conditioned on cross-task precedents and lessons, turn-level reflection, and future hindsight from the completed trajectory, and the resulting distribution is distilled back via on-policy self-distillation. The experience bank grows across rounds and the retrospective context is refreshed, enabling co-evolution of model, data, and supervision; a stronger frontier model proposes constrained edits to how privileged context is constructed.

**Background**: Self-evolving agents aim to improve from their own experience after deployment, but naturally collected trajectories often lack ground-truth solutions or verifier-derived rewards, making reinforcement learning difficult. ## [BenchDoor: Poisoning Attacks That Exploit Benchmark Incentives](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.27533) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduce BenchDoor, a family of data poisoning attacks that implant backdoors while simultaneously improving benchmark scores, achieving positive benchmark gains in all 30 evaluated configurations and held-out attack success rates of 82.33% to 100.00% at poisoning rates of 2% to 10% across Qwen and Gemma models. This work shows that benchmarks themselves can serve as attack vectors, undermining the integrity of ML evaluation and potentially allowing poisoned models or datasets to be adopted because they appear to improve benchmark performance. The attack formalizes five scenarios, including manipulating benchmark training or test data and supplying an independent training dataset, and remains effective after synthetic data generation and similarity-based decontamination, with attack success rates of at least 90.33%.

## [Native safety can be transferred from small teachers to larger students via on-policy distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.27555) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper introduces the 'native safety reuse' problem and shows that safety acquired during pretraining can be transferred from a small safety-pretrained teacher to standard-pretrained students through on-policy distillation with cross-tokenizer alignment. The resulting 1.7B student shows only a 5.00% average attack success rate increase after fine-tuning (vs. 11.58% for safety post-training) while retaining 48.20% average utility, far above the teacher's 27.42%. This reframes safety as a reusable model property rather than something permanently tied to the original pretrained model, enabling selective small-to-large safety transfer without inheriting the teacher's utility limitations. It could make robust safety more accessible to model developers who cannot afford expensive safety pretraining from scratch. The method has the student generate responses to safety-pretraining prompts while the teacher supervises token-level predictions along the student's own trajectories, and cross-tokenizer alignment enables transfer across model families. Unlike conventional large-to-small distillation, this framework enables selective small-to-large safety transfer, though results are from an early-stage preprint and may need broader validation.

## [Masked Diffusion LMs Form Factual Access States in First Attention Layer](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.27580) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.27580) finds that masked diffusion language models (DLMs) assemble a 'factual access state' in the first attention layer, where relation wording is fused into the visible entity's position, unlike autoregressive (AR) models that perform relation-specific selection later at the readout position. The authors leverage this state for knowledge editing (Multi-View Edit) and training-free retrieval, showing substantial gains on paraphrase and reverse question answering where AR editors fail. This mechanistic finding reveals a fundamental architectural difference in how DLMs store and retrieve factual knowledge, with direct implications for knowledge editing and retrieval-augmented generation. It suggests that editing and retrieval methods designed for AR models may not transfer directly to DLMs, and that DLMs offer new opportunities for more robust factual manipulation. The factual access state varies with the relation's surface form and query direction, so queries about one fact occupy a region of state space rather than a single point; Multi-View Edit fits one shared value per direction across that region and installs it in the early-MLP block. For retrieval, the state at each entity position serves as a relation-specific retrieval vector without training, returning both pieces of evidence for two-entity queries where pooled, prompted, and lexical retrievers almost never return both.

## [Audit Finds Recursive Self-Improvement Studies Overclaim Product Evidence, Underspecify Process](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.27610) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A systematic audit of 114 studies, including 90 self-described recursive self-improvement (RSI) papers, found that 90% report product evaluation but only 60% report evaluation on tasks unused for selection, and only 22% audit two or more reruns of the full loop. Among 26 studies claiming a better improvement procedure, only 4 compared earlier and later procedures from identical starting artifacts at a matched budget. The findings expose a gap between RSI claims and the evidence supporting them, showing that repeatability and improved-procedure evidence lag behind product evaluation. This matters for AI evaluation methodology and for anyone assessing claims about self-evolving LLM agents, as it supports a claim-indexed reporting standard linking each claim to the evaluation design needed to test it. The audit used full-text coding of 114 eligible studies in a reproducible arXiv search frame frozen in October 2026, with independent human coding, third-reader adjudication, and blind coding of improver comparisons to assess reliability. A human-coded random sample confirmed the contrast: 45% evaluated on tasks unused for selection and 14% audited two or more reruns.

Researchers present a system where a single $122 head-mounted camera reads printed fiducial markers on a $22 electronics-free glove against paper tiles, replacing the wrist camera, pose tracker, and multiple data streams in handheld robot demonstration devices. The labels achieve 6.5 mm and 1.6° median accuracy against robot encoders with 93–100% frame coverage, and a policy trained on them pays only 3% in validation loss. This approach drastically lowers the cost and complexity of collecting robot learning data by eliminating sensors and synchronization overhead, making high-quality demonstration data more accessible. It could accelerate imitation learning research and deployment by allowing anyone with a cheap camera and glove to gather data that rivals teleoperation. At deployment, the same head camera is mounted on a $120 arm that mimics the collector's head from the robot's joint state; adding 194 glove demonstrations to 48 teleoperated episodes lifts rollout success from 10/25 to 17/25, matching 172 teleoperated episodes alone (18/25). The full co-trained head-camera policy succeeds in 20/25 trials, versus 15/25 for a wrist-camera recipe that drops objects when the goal leaves view, and 12/25 for a fixed camera.

The paper introduces Bayes-Consistent Tempering (BCT), a method that makes temperature explicit in both the distributions and dynamics of flow language models, fixing mismatches caused by post-hoc temperature scaling. Experiments on hyperspherical and von Mises–Fisher flow LMs show that BCT improves GSM8K generation across a broad temperature range and also benefits Sudoku, with the learned variant being more robust at very low temperatures. This work addresses a specific reliability issue in flow language models, where lowering temperature does not consistently improve reasoning performance as it does in discrete diffusion models. By making temperature a property of the generative flow, BCT could lead to more controllable and robust text generation, especially for reasoning tasks, and may encourage rethinking temperature handling in other continuous generative models. BCT trains the denoiser on tempered intermediate states and tempers the endpoint distribution using corresponding tempered dynamics; training-free variants are also derived for conventionally trained checkpoints. The learned realization outperforms training-free variants at very low temperatures, and code and model weights are available at the project page.

An ablation study of a production speech-to-QA pipeline found that enabling the transcript-rewrite preprocessing stage lowers downstream retrieval accuracy by 0.061, even though the same stage raises corpus quality as judged by four LLM judges and six human experts. ## [RLSplat: Resource-Linear Budget Control for Feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.27712) ⭐️ 7.0/10

RLSplat introduces a resource-linear budget-controllable feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting framework where representation size, inference latency, and peak memory all scale linearly with the Gaussian budget, unlike prior methods that prune dense predictions at near-constant cost. It learns a Gaussian allocation policy to distribute the budget across local scene regions and uses resource-linear Gaussian decoding with hierarchical neighbor search. This addresses a key gap in budget-controllable FF3DGS by making inference cost itself scale with the budget, which is crucial for deployment on resource-constrained devices. It outperforms prior methods at every budget, surpassing the strongest baseline even with 4× fewer Gaussians, and runs up to 4.1× faster with 9.6× less peak memory at low budgets. RLSplat generates exactly the requested number of Gaussians via a learned allocation policy and refines them with resource-linear decoding where each Gaussian attends only to nearby Gaussians found by efficient hierarchical neighbor search. In zero-shot evaluation, it surpasses the strongest baseline even with 4× fewer Gaussians and achieves up to 4.1× faster runtime with 9.6× less peak memory at low budgets.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 22, 04:00

**Background**: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) is a rasterization-based technique for real-time radiance field rendering that represents scenes as collections of 3D Gaussians, enabling high-quality novel view synthesis from images. Feed-forward 3DGS (FF3DGS) reconstructs 3D scenes in a single forward pass, making it suitable for resource-constrained applications. Recent budget-controllable FF3DGS methods allow adjusting the number of Gaussians at inference to meet storage or latency constraints, but they typically predict a dense set and then prune, incurring near-constant inference cost regardless of the budget.

## [World2HOSI orchestrates experts for long-horizon human-object-scene interaction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.27725) ⭐️ 7.0/10

World2HOSI introduces a multi-expert orchestration harness that generates continuous human-object-scene interaction (HOSI) data from 3D Gaussian Splatting scenes and natural language instructions. The key insight is that long-horizon HOSI is better achieved by orchestrating existing specialized experts around a shared, persistent scene state than by training a single unified model. This approach addresses the data scarcity problem in embodied AI by leveraging existing HOI and HSI models without costly unified training. It could influence future work in embodied AI, animation, and game development by demonstrating that orchestration over a shared scene state outperforms monolithic models. The harness plans action stages over a persistent scene state built from decoupled background and object assets, invokes experts via their native conditioning interfaces, and writes effects back to the state. Bounded residual optimization and contact-driven physics simulation are used to reduce physical artifacts while preserving interaction intent.

## [Framing and Elicitation Shape How LLMs Update Probabilities](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.27745) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.27745) tests how seven LLM configurations update probability estimates when given a single new piece of information, varying whether the update is stated directly or merely reported by someone else, and whether the model gives one probability or five weighted estimates. Under stated, direct elicitation all seven models move in the annotated direction by 18–28 percentage points, but reporting the information lowers this movement in all seven (significantly in six) and increases reverse movements. As LLMs are increasingly used as judgment assistants and as stand-in participants in psychology experiments, this work shows that simple framing choices—stated versus reported evidence—can systematically bias how much models revise their beliefs. It also warns that elicitation formats which reduce extreme probability values may simultaneously reduce sensitivity to evidence, so the two properties must be evaluated separately. The study pairs premise-hypothesis items from δ-SNLI with one strengthener and one weakener each, elicits prior and posterior in separate calls, and measures directional movement s with the prior canceled out; it uses two local models (Qwen3-8B, OLMo-2-7B; 240 pairs) and five agent command-line harness configurations (120 pairs), with hypotheses and analysis rules fixed before formal runs but not publicly registered. Because δ-SNLI annotates only direction, the authors make no claim about how large an update should be.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 22, 04:00

**Background**: δ-SNLI is a variant of the Stanford Natural Language Inference (SNLI) dataset that annotates the direction in which a premise-hypothesis relationship changes when additional evidence is added. Large language models are probabilistic next-token predictors, but researchers increasingly probe whether they behave like Bayesian reasoners that adjust beliefs in response to new information. Qwen3-8B and OLMo-2-7B are two open-weight 7–8B-parameter models used here as test subjects, with the latter from the Allen Institute for AI's fully open OLMo 2 family.

## [RELAY: Hybrid LLM Rules and Agents Restore Historical Builds](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.27784) ⭐️ 7.0/10

RELAY presents a hybrid framework that uses an LLM to derive reusable deterministic repair rules for historical build failures, escalates unresolved cases to a per-case agent, and demonstrates full automation on 14,159 OSS-Fuzz cases. This approach addresses environment decay in historical builds, which affects 69.7% of OSS-Fuzz cases, and shows that reusable rules combined with agent escalation restore more builds at lower cost than either method alone, impacting vulnerability benchmarking and software engineering research. Rule derivation can be fully automated, and reusable rules restore as many builds as per-case agents with fewer build executions, but agents are still needed for cases that rules cannot handle; the hybrid approach outperforms both individually.

## [SLM-SS: Token-Based Speech Separation with Speech Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.27785) ⭐️ 7.0/10

SLM-SS introduces a token-based generative speech separation framework that uses neural codecs to discretize clean speech into multi-codebook token sequences and serializes multi-speaker targets via Serialized Output Training (SOT). An encoder-decoder autoregressive speech language model predicts the zero-order sequence for speaker ordering and coarse linguistic content, while a non-autoregressive module refines higher-order residual codebooks; on Libri2Mix, the per-talker NAR variant achieves 6.92% WER, approaching codec-only reconstruction. Most existing speech separation systems are optimized for signal-level metrics and can produce waveforms that score well but are suboptimal for intelligibility-sensitive downstream tasks such as ASR. SLM-SS shifts the objective toward discrete linguistic tokens, and its WavTokenizer variant achieves the highest mean subjective quality score among evaluated systems, with UTMOS and DNSMOS advantages over discriminative baselines persisting on unseen noisy and Chinese mixtures without fine-tuning. The framework relies on multi-codebook neural codec tokens and a two-stage design: an autoregressive SLM handles the zero-order codebook, and a non-autoregressive module refines residual codebooks; a per-talker NAR strategy simplifies high-order modeling and improves stability. The WavTokenizer variant eliminates NAR refinement entirely and still achieves the best subjective quality, though the reported 6.92% WER is on Libri2Mix and broader benchmark validation remains to be seen.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 22, 04:00

**Background**: Speech separation aims to isolate individual speakers from a mixed audio signal, and neural network-based methods have substantially improved signal-level metrics in recent years. Neural audio codecs convert continuous waveforms into discrete tokens using learned codebooks, enabling speech to be modeled with language-model-style architectures. Serialized Output Training (SOT) represents multiple overlapping speakers as a single serialized token stream rather than parallel output branches, and has shown state-of-the-art results in multi-talker speech recognition.

## [SMART: Segment-Level Rubric Framework for Semantic ASR Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.27820) ⭐️ 7.0/10

SMART introduces a segment-level, context-aware rubric-based framework for traceable semantic evaluation of ASR transcripts, along with a new metric called Semantic Impact Error Rate (SIER). It achieves 0.843 F1 against majority-vote human labels, outperforming direct LLM judgment (0.745 F1). This work moves beyond traditional Word Error Rate (WER) by assessing the semantic consequences of ASR errors, enabling more meaningful evaluation and targeted correction. It could benefit speech recognition researchers and practitioners who need to measure and improve the real-world impact of transcription errors. SMART maps reference-hypothesis discrepancies into coherent segments and applies a structured contextual rubric to assign explicit consequence labels, supporting SIER at utterance, chunk, and lexical levels. Evaluation across multiple LLMs shows relative insensitivity to the choice of evaluation model, and a target-reference-free rubric for correction reduces MER by 0.85-0.98 and SIER_lex by 1.18-1.65 percentage points.
