**Background**: Word Error Rate (WER) is the dominant metric for evaluating automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems, calculated as the sum of substitutions, deletions, and insertions divided by the number of words in the reference transcript. However, WER treats all lexical edits equally, ignoring that some errors change meaning while others do not. Recent research has explored using large language models (LLMs) for semantic evaluation of transcripts, but direct LLM judgment can be inconsistent and lacks traceability.

## [Study Maps Hallucinations in LLM Cross-Language Code Translation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.27868) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper presents a systematic empirical study of hallucinations in LLM-based cross-language code translation, covering three benchmark datasets, six language pairs, and seven LLMs. The authors manually annotate 13,919 hallucination cases to build a three-category taxonomy (Semantic Consistency Conflicts, Factual Knowledge Conflicts, and Project Context Deviations) and propose HaluCodeTran, a mitigation framework combining BM25-based retrieval of translation examples with taxonomy-aware reflective refinement. Code translation is increasingly used for real-world migration and modernization, where a small semantic deviation can silently change program behavior, so characterizing and mitigating these hallucinations is essential for building trustworthy LLM-based migration tools. The work fills a gap left by prior hallucination studies that focused mainly on natural-language generation or code generation rather than translation. The taxonomy is grounded in execution-tested analysis and examines how hallucination types vary across models, datasets, and translation directions, providing a practical baseline for more reliable code migration. The mitigation framework relies on retrieval of relevant translation examples and reflective refinement rather than model retraining, though the abstract does not report quantitative effectiveness numbers.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 22, 04:00

**Background**: In AI, a hallucination is output that contains false or misleading information presented as fact; in code generation, prior work has built taxonomies of hallucinated code such as fabricated APIs or incorrect logic. Cross-language code translation asks a model to rewrite a program from one programming language into another while preserving its functionality, and benchmarks such as PolyHumanEval evaluate this task across many languages. Because translation errors can be subtle and compile successfully, they are harder to catch than obvious generation failures.

## [DPO Hyperparameters Shift with Scale and Resist Transfer, Study Finds](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.27895) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.27895) empirically maps the DPO hyperparameter landscape using a dense grid across model scales, showing that optimal learning rates vary with model size and that hyperparameters do not transfer across training datasets. It also finds that validation loss is a poor proxy for downstream performance and that short candidate training runs can substantially cut the cost of hyperparameter selection. DPO is a widely used post-training method, yet practitioners often assume hyperparameters can be transferred from smaller runs or other datasets; this work shows such assumptions fail, which could change how teams budget and design hyperparameter tuning for alignment. The finding that validation loss weakly correlates with downstream benchmark optima is particularly consequential for anyone using loss-based early stopping or model selection. The study uses a dense hyperparameter grid across models from the same family, leverages intermediate checkpoints as an inexpensive signal, and compares static versus dynamic benchmarks to identify which provide the strongest selection signal. It also evaluates state-of-the-art HPO strategies in this setting and releases all training configurations and evaluation results for reproducibility.

## [ReCam: Stable Long Video Generation with Full Context Memory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.27986) ⭐️ 7.0/10

ReCam proposes grouping local spatiotemporal blocks of historical latents into vectors and projecting them into a Diffusion Transformer's hidden space as memory tokens, enabling full-history access with reduced token count. It also introduces dual-pointer denoising with separate noise schedules for recent context and target frames, achieving an 80.1 VBench-Long overall score and a clothing consistency of 4.09 versus 3.03 for the best baseline. This work addresses a key bottleneck in long-horizon video generation—the growing cost of conditioning on expanding history—by offering a memory mechanism that retains full context without prohibitive token overhead. The state-of-the-art VBench-Long score and strong off-screen subject reappearance consistency suggest practical improvements for generating coherent long videos, which could benefit content creation, simulation, and streaming applications. ReCam reduces token count by grouping historical latents into block-level memory tokens processed via native self-attention, and mitigates temporal drift during autoregressive rollout with dual-pointer denoising using separate noise schedules. It leads on all four consistency metrics for off-screen subject reappearance on R2M-Bench, though the abstract does not specify computational costs or maximum video length.

## [OPTD Aligns Layer-wise Log-Probability Transitions for On-Policy Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28048) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces On-Policy Transition Distillation (OPTD), which augments standard final-layer distribution matching in on-policy distillation by aligning teacher and student layer-to-layer log-probability increments on student-generated rollouts. Across three backbones and eight benchmarks, OPTD achieves best or tied-best overall performance, recovering about 90% of the teacher-student capability gap in a three-domain setting versus about 75% for standard OPD. This work shows that intermediate-layer prediction transitions provide additional task-relevant supervision beyond final-layer matching, offering a practical way to improve knowledge distillation for large language models. It could benefit researchers and practitioners working on model compression and multi-domain distillation, where closing the teacher-student gap is critical. A diagnostic study found that stronger teacher-student agreement in intermediate transitions correlates with higher answer correctness, with correct responses showing lower mean transition KL across all measured intermediate layer pairs. OPTD is evaluated in both dual- and three-domain distillation settings, but the abstract does not specify the model sizes or the computational overhead of aligning multiple layer pairs.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 22, 04:00

**Background**: Knowledge distillation trains a smaller student model to mimic a larger teacher model, typically by matching the teacher's output distribution on fixed data. On-policy distillation instead trains the student on its own generated sequences and uses the teacher's feedback on those sequences, which helps address distribution mismatch. Layer-wise distillation methods have explored matching intermediate representations, but aligning layer-to-layer prediction changes (transitions) on student rollouts is a newer direction.

## [Training-Free Linker Lets Streaming Diarizers Track More Speakers Than Slots](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28053) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper introduces a causal, training-free linker that allows frozen streaming diarizers, such as Streaming Sortformer, to track more speakers than their fixed number of output slots. By relabeling slot posteriors with an off-the-shelf speaker encoder, it reduces the diarization error rate (DER) above the slot cap from 36.8% to 22.6% on 1,418 sessions across eight corpora. This work addresses a fundamental limitation of streaming diarization systems—fixed speaker slots—without requiring retraining, making it practical for real-world deployments where the number of speakers is unknown and can exceed the model's capacity. The approach could improve transcription and meeting analysis in scenarios with many participants, such as courtroom hearings, where it reduced cpWER from 82.7% to 24.4%. The linker operates only on the host's slot posteriors and audio: it keeps frames where one slot is active, splits each slot at speaker changes, embeds each piece with an off-the-shelf speaker encoder, and matches against a bank of speakers seen so far. Because it only relabels, missed speech and false alarm rates remain identical to the host's, so all gains come from reduced speaker confusion; the same constants transfer to an 8-slot successor and two streaming EEND hosts from a different model family.

**Background**: Speaker diarization is the task of partitioning an audio stream into segments according to speaker identity, answering "who spoke when?". The diarization error rate (DER) is the standard metric, combining missed speech, false alarms, and speaker confusion; cpWER is a related metric for speaker-attributed word error rate.

A new arXiv paper audits Concept Bottleneck Models (CBMs) and Concept Embedding Models (CEMs) on the CUB-200-2011 benchmark, finding that task and concept accuracy do not guarantee predictions are based on exposed concepts. This work challenges the evaluation paradigm for interpretable ML, showing that standard accuracy metrics can mask whether models truly rely on human-interpretable concepts. It cautions researchers against overinterpreting accuracy gaps on CUB and calls for more rigorous auditing of concept-based models. The CUB annotations are noisy: class-level labels agree with per-image annotations on only ~82% of image-concept pairs, and classifiers trained on per-image annotations reach only ~37% species accuracy. Ablations show that restricting a ResNet50 backbone to local BagNet patches lowers accuracy recoverable from concept scores from 72% to 43%, and localization/occlusion analyses reveal that local concept scores often use the head as a proxy for other body parts.

A new arXiv paper argues that continuous-time graph learning should identify low-dimensional predictive states sufficient for future prediction rather than reconstructing full interaction histories. The intrinsic predictive dimension is estimated by removing the history-independent marginal from the history-conditioned future distribution, decomposing the predictive residual operator, and finding the minimum effective rank that preserves the full history's predictive power. ## [Dynamic Expert Skipping in MoEs Fails to Beat Simple Static Baseline](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28369) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.28369) benchmarks four representative dynamic expert-skipping methods for Mixture-of-Experts models against a simple static baseline that reduces the number of active experts k uniformly across all layers and tokens. At matched expert-compute budgets on Gemma4-26B-A4B, Qwen3-30B-A3B, and Qwen3-VL, the static baseline is hard to outperform consistently, and dynamic methods often underperform it. This controlled comparison challenges the growing line of MoE dynamic expert-skipping research by showing that a calibration-free static-k reduction is a strong competitor, suggesting that reported gains may partly stem from unfair comparisons. It urges the ML efficiency community to adopt matched-compute static controls as a mandatory baseline before claiming improvements. The paper unifies four prior methods under a taxonomy and finds that the effective k achieved during calibration can diverge from the effective k at test time, causing over- or under-estimation of inference compute. It recommends a calibration-free per-modality static k reduction and validates this on a held-out model and modality.

VisualEvolve introduces a self-evolving framework that refines executable visual operations and tool-use strategies for vision-language models through a Select-Execute-Evolve-Evaluate cycle without updating model parameters. It improves over the initial skill library in 23 of 24 settings across four VLM backbones and six evaluation sets, with a maximum gain of 15.1 percentage points on VisualProbe Hard using Qwen3.5-Plus. This work addresses key challenges in visual tool use for VLMs, such as performance regression during skill refinement and evolution evidence overload, by introducing Skill-Library Snapshot Selection and Progressive Evidence Access. Skill-Library Snapshot Selection uses a fixed validation set disjoint from execution tasks to pick an effective historical snapshot, limiting performance regression propagation. Progressive Evidence Access guides capability-gap diagnosis through a coarse-to-fine hierarchy of Skill-Performance Report, Evolution Log, Trajectory Summaries, and raw trajectory segments; ablation studies confirm the contributions of both components, and skills can be reused across backbones.

A new arXiv preprint (2610.28397) introduces MAS-Guard, a unified framework that safeguards both single-agent and multi-agent LLM applications, including opaque agents that cannot be instrumented. It combines a local Agent Guardrail (A-Guard) layer with system-level Agent Charters and a Control Plane, and reduces attack success rates by 71.5–86.3% across six benchmarks while maintaining utility on benign tasks. As agentic AI systems move from generating text to planning and executing workflows, and as multi-agent architectures introduce distributed authority and potentially compromised participants, fragmented defenses leave critical gaps. MAS-Guard offers a unified approach that could become a foundation for securing enterprise and open multi-agent deployments against unsafe actions, data leakage, and adversarial manipulation. The framework enforces a shared set of interventions—allow, reflection, confirmation, and block—and was evaluated on six benchmarks using three agent LLMs from different providers. ## [Base Models Outperform Instruction-Tuned Versions on Factual Recall, Coining 'Instruction Tax'](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28407) ⭐️ 7.0/10

In the AKBC LM-KBC 2026 Shared Task, the authors achieved a leaderboard score of 0.6836 using a base model with text-completion prompting, more than double the baseline of 0.2964 and significantly higher than the 0.5681 obtained by the instruction-tuned chat version of the same model. They attribute this gap to an 'instruction tax'—a drop in factual recall caused by instruction tuning itself, rooted in the model's weights rather than the prompting method. This finding challenges the common assumption that instruction-tuned chat models are strictly better for knowledge-intensive tasks, suggesting that practitioners should consider base models with completion-style prompts for factual recall. It has practical implications for prompt engineering and model selection in closed-book knowledge base construction and other recall-focused applications. The method prompts the base model with a few training examples, generates 64–256 outputs, and retains only repeated answers; two relation-specific techniques further improve recall for large answer sets and verify a person's vitality before predicting their place of death. The result is from a single shared task with models up to 32B parameters and no retrieval or fine-tuning, so generalization to other tasks and model sizes remains to be tested.

## [WorldSR: Entity-Aligned World Knowledge Retrieval for Grounded Super-Resolution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28423) ⭐️ 7.0/10

WorldSR introduces a framework that augments super-resolution (SR) with explicit, entity-aligned visual world knowledge by decomposing inputs into semantic entities and performing entity-wise retrieval of structurally and semantically aligned reference images from a large external corpus. It adds a memory mechanism to reuse prior retrievals and a multi-step filtering process, then integrates selected references through a novel multi-reference SR model, outperforming existing generative SR methods on real-world benchmarks. Generative-prior SR methods are stochastic, tied to their base model, costly to update, and prone to hallucination as real-world data evolves; WorldSR's entity-level grounding offers a simple, effective complement that improves structural fidelity and visual quality. This retrieval-augmented approach could influence how SR systems are designed for reliability in real-world deployment. The method relies on a large-scale external image corpus and a multi-step filtering pipeline to refine candidate references, with a memory mechanism to avoid redundant retrieval; the final multi-reference SR model uses the selected references as fine-grained constraints for detail synthesis and structural recovery. Experiments are conducted on real-world SR benchmarks, though the abstract does not specify corpus size, retrieval latency, or performance on non-entity or heavily degraded inputs.

The paper proposes TaskWAM, a closed-loop, stage-aware framework that uses Mode Tokens to encode fine-grained task requirements and State Tokens to track execution progress, forming a structured task state that steers World-Action Models toward task-intended futures. It also introduces StageBench, a controlled multi-stage manipulation benchmark with parameterized stage variations and automated evaluation. This work addresses Stage Confusion, a real failure mode in long-horizon manipulation where locally plausible rollouts drift toward the wrong task stage, and its plug-and-play transfer across heterogeneous WAM architectures and embodiments (single-arm, dual-arm grippers, dexterous hands, humanoids) could make stage-aware steering a general component for embodied generalist policies. TaskWAM is evaluated on both simulation benchmarks and real-world tasks, showing reduced confusion and competitive performance with state-of-the-art methods; the new StageBench provides controlled multi-stage variations with automated evaluation, though the abstract does not report specific success-rate numbers or computational overhead.

## [REACT: VLM-Guided Contact Retargeting for Humanoid-Human Interaction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28523) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers present REACT, a framework that learns deployable humanoid-human interaction policies from human-human demonstrations by treating semantic contact structure as the key supervisory signal. A VLM-guided contact modeling and retargeting pipeline identifies meaningful contacts and transfers them onto humanoid-human geometry, and privileged interaction policies are distilled into egocentric depth policies trained entirely from onboard sensing. The method is evaluated in simulation and on a real Unitree G1 humanoid across five contact-rich interactions, performing all five on hardware using onboard sensing alone. Humanoid-human interaction is a hard problem because close physical contact causes severe occlusion and partial observability, which breaks pose estimation and typically requires external tracking or privileged human state. REACT shows that semantic contact modeling plus generative partner-state modeling can enable deployable policies that rely only on onboard sensing, a step toward real-world humanoid collaboration without instrumented environments. The framework uses interaction-aware contact rewards to learn physically grounded behaviors in a privileged stage, then distills them into egocentric depth policies trained with photorealistic human depth rendering. Generative partner-state modeling objectives predict partner motion from occluded egocentric views, improving contact recall on four of five interactions, most notably under heavy occlusion; semantic contact modeling substantially improves preservation of demonstrated interactions.

**Background**: Vision-language models (VLMs) are multimodal generative models that jointly reason over images and text, and are increasingly used in robotics to ground semantic understanding. Motion retargeting transfers human motion onto a robot's morphology, while privileged imitation learning trains a teacher policy with access to extra state information and distills it into a student policy that uses only deployable observations. Humanoid-human interaction adds mutual occlusion between partners, which corrupts both pose estimation and the motion-capture data used for learning.

## [Binary Discrete Diffusion Uses Candidate Sets for Logic and Planning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28543) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces Binary Discrete Diffusion, a continuous-time discrete diffusion process whose noisy state is a per-position set of candidate tokens encoded as a binary membership vector, allowing information to be lost and recovered gradually. It outperforms well-tuned masked and uniform diffusion baselines on Sudoku-Extreme, Boxoban, and graph coloring under matched architectures and budgets, with the largest gains on the hardest instances. This work shows that the corruption kernel can materially change what the reverse model learns, offering a more expressive intermediate representation for iterative reasoning and constrained generation. It could influence the design of discrete diffusion models for planning, coding, and math tasks where partial uncertainty must be represented explicitly. Binary diffusion changes candidate sets through additions and removals rather than erasing a token's identity in one corruption event, and the symmetric formulation remains competitive on language modeling benchmarks (Text8, TinyStories, OpenWebText). The gains are largest on the hardest instances, though the approach is evaluated under controlled training, sampling, and tuning budgets rather than at large scale.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 22, 04:00

**Background**: Discrete diffusion models iteratively denoise a noisy sequence of categorical data such as text, enabling any-order generation with self-correction and in-filling. In masked and uniform diffusion, a token's identity is erased in a single corruption event, so noisy states cannot explicitly represent partially resolved uncertainty where several alternatives remain plausible. Continuous-time discrete diffusion formulates the forward process as a continuous-time Markov chain over a finite state space, and this paper replaces the per-position categorical state with a binary membership vector over candidate tokens.

## [Learned Wiring: Biologically Inspired Architecture Boosts Sample Efficiency](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28555) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces Learned Wiring (LeWi), a neural architecture where each neuron has a learned low-dimensional embedding and connects only to nearby neurons, with embeddings and weights trained jointly. Benchmarked on CSFRBench, LeWi achieves 27% lower mean learning-curve area than dense networks across 32 targets and outperforms the dense baseline on 16 of 17 world-model prediction tasks. This work addresses the gap between theory and practice in exploiting compositional sparsity for sample-efficient learning, showing that jointly learning connectivity and weights can realize theoretical benefits. It offers a promising direction for improving data efficiency in deep learning, particularly for tasks with hierarchical or modular structure. LeWi's advantage is most pronounced on targets with hierarchical structure, intermediate reuse, or independent modules, while dense networks perform better on targets with a single high-arity function. The benchmark CSFRBench hides the target's compositional computation during training but retains it for diagnosis, enabling controlled evaluation.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 22, 04:00

**Background**: High-dimensional statistical learning suffers from the curse of dimensionality, but many real-world functions are compositionally sparse—they decompose into local functions of few variables, which can reduce sample complexity. However, exploiting this hidden structure with gradient-based training is challenging, and dense networks often fail to realize the theoretical benefits. LeWi is inspired by the spatial organization of biological neural circuits, where neurons connect primarily to nearby neurons.

## [Classical Feature Selection Beats 7B LLM Selectors in 18-Dataset Study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28556) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A systematic empirical study across 18 datasets compared five classical statistical feature selectors against frozen Qwen2.5-7B and Llama-3.3-70B selectors and two GRPO-tuned Qwen2.5-7B models, finding that classical selectors generally achieve higher predictive performance (ROC-AUC for classification, R² for regression) under a pre-specified ~33% feature budget with strict train-only fitting. The negative result is a useful caution for practitioners tempted to replace established statistical feature selection with LLM-based selectors on tabular data, suggesting that semantic feature names alone do not yet justify the added cost and complexity of 7B-scale models. The framework used 10 datasets for GRPO training, 2 for checkpoint validation, and 6 held-out evaluation datasets across five seeded partitions; a cardinality-matched semantic sensitivity experiment showed that informative feature names improved zero-shot Qwen-7B regression R² by +0.1964 versus anonymized names and +0.1606 versus shuffled names, while classification gains were smaller (+0.0159 and +0.0084 ROC-AUC) and dataset-dependent.

## [Teacher's Myopic Scoring Blamed for Agentic Distillation Failures, New Repair Method Proposed](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28586) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.28586) challenges the compounding-error explanation for failures in agentic on-policy distillation (OPD), arguing instead that the teacher's myopic next-token scoring is the culprit. The authors propose Rollout-to-Scorer Distillation (R2S), a reward-free method that repairs the teacher's scorer before distillation by mining high-disagreement states and fine-tuning the teacher on takeover-informed scores. This work identifies a fundamental flaw in how teacher models score tokens during agentic OPD, potentially reshaping how researchers design distillation pipelines for LLM agents. The proposed R2S method outperforms three state-of-the-art agentic-OPD methods across all twelve teacher-student-environment combinations, suggesting broad applicability. R2S mines high-disagreement states from the untrained student, runs teacher takeovers, and keeps states where enough takeovers pass a reward-free check (consensus or LLM judge), then fine-tunes the teacher to give takeover-informed scores on every assistant token from the divergence turn onward without the takeover in context. The repaired teacher is frozen as the sole scorer for standard OPD, requiring no task reward during repair or training, and achieves a 12.8 success-point average improvement over the best baseline in each cell.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 22, 04:00

**Background**: Agentic on-policy distillation trains a student agent on its own trajectories while a teacher scores every token, providing dense supervision. A common explanation for failures is compounding error: the student's mistakes lead it into states where the teacher is unreliable. This paper argues that even when the teacher can recover from such states, its next-token scores fail to penalize delaying moves that outcome-based reinforcement learning would punish, a discrepancy termed the rollout-scorer gap.

## [SAGE uses LLMs to evolve symbolic acceleration inequalities for MILP](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.11850) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduced SAGE (Symbolic Acceleration via Generative Evolution), a framework that uses LLM agents guided by evolutionary search to automatically discover reusable acceleration inequality families for mixed-integer linear programming (MILP). Across seven MILP benchmarks, SAGE reduced optimality gaps by up to 62.1% relative to baseline formulations under a fixed time budget and reached target gaps up to 5.51× faster. Designing acceleration inequalities has traditionally required deep mathematical expertise and manual effort, limiting solver improvements to specialists. SAGE automates this creative process at the modeling level, potentially making advanced solver tuning accessible to non-experts and improving performance across a wide range of combinatorial optimization tasks. SAGE initializes candidate inequality families with an LLM, screens them for admissibility on a small development set (checking solution feasibility and separation from the relaxation solution), and iteratively refines them via evolutionary crossover and mutation agents. Notably, candidates are selected through empirical screening rather than formal mathematical proofs, and ablations show robustness across different LLM backends, solvers, and internal cut settings.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 22, 04:00

**Background**: Integer programming (IP) and its mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) variant are NP-hard problems central to combinatorial optimization, often solved by branch-and-bound algorithms. A common way to speed up solvers is to add valid inequalities (cuts) that tighten the linear relaxation, but designing such inequality families manually is a creative, expertise-intensive task. Recent work has explored using large language models (LLMs) within evolutionary search to automate algorithm and heuristic discovery, and SAGE applies this paradigm to symbolic discovery of acceleration inequalities.

EMMA introduces a framework combining a diffusion Transformer-based generative data engine, DreamTransfer, with an adaptive training pipeline, AdaMix, to augment vision-language-action (VLA) robotic control policies. Evaluations show a 92% relative performance increase over training with real data alone in zero-shot visual settings, with an additional 17% improvement from AdaMix. The approach could reduce reliance on real-world data collection and accelerate deployment of robust robotic policies. DreamTransfer generates multi-view consistent and geometrically plausible manipulation videos with text-driven editing of foreground, background, and lighting while preserving 3D structure. AdaMix adaptively weights samples based on policy performance to emphasize challenging samples, and the framework supports both real-to-real and sim-to-real transfer.

## [Reward Model Accuracy Fails as Selection Criterion for Personalized Alignment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.23067) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2512.23067) demonstrates that standard reward model (RM) accuracy is a poor predictor of downstream performance when using reward-guided decoding (RGD) for personalized LLM alignment. The authors introduce policy accuracy as a better metric and Pref-LaMP, the first personalized alignment benchmark with ground-truth user completions, showing that RM accuracy correlates only weakly with policy accuracy (Kendall's tau = 0.08–0.31). This finding challenges the dominant practice of optimizing reward model accuracy as a proxy for personalized behavior, revealing that the field may be optimizing for metrics that do not predict deployment performance. Practitioners deploying personalized LLMs with inference-time adaptation need to reconsider model selection criteria, as methods with 20-point RM accuracy differences produce nearly identical output quality. The paper shows a complete decoupling between discriminative ranking and generation metrics: high-ranking accuracy can fail to generate behaviorally aligned responses, while simple in-context learning (ICL) dominates all reward-guided methods for models ≥3B parameters, achieving ~3 point ROUGE-1 gains over the best reward method at 7B scale. The correlation between upstream RM accuracy and downstream policy accuracy is measured by Kendall's tau, a rank correlation statistic.

In deployment, computational constraints often require inference-time adaptation like reward-guided decoding (RGD), where the reward model steers generation step-by-step, rather than fine-tuning a separate policy per user. Kendall's tau is a statistic measuring ordinal association between two rankings, with values near zero indicating weak correlation.

## [Agents-as-Peers: Bias-Controlled Multi-Agent Peer Assessment for LLM Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.02589) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces Agents-as-Peers, a distributed multi-agent peer-assessment protocol where every LLM generates tasks, answers a shared task set, and judges peers' answers, with no privileged evaluator. In an instantiation with 12 LLMs and 420 agent-generated questions, it aggregates 55,440 non-self peer judgments per regime and measures self-bias, identity effects, presentation-position sensitivity, and judge severity. This approach addresses benchmark staleness and judge bias by replacing fixed benchmarks and centralized judges with a cohort-relative peer-assessment protocol that explicitly reports biases alongside rankings. It could improve the reliability and transparency of LLM evaluation, affecting researchers and practitioners who rely on benchmarks to compare models. Peer scores align strongly with accuracy on TruthfulQA (Pearson r=0.904) and GSM8K (r=0.873), and on TruthfulQA the peer-score correlation is substantially higher than the self-score correlation (r=0.538). The study also finds that most agents assign their own answers higher scores, visible identity changes scores for some agents, the first fixed answer slot yields scores 0.39 points higher than a shuffled baseline, and judges differ markedly in severity.

## [TabProbe Uses Tabular Foundation Models to Learn Association Rules](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.14622) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduce a model-agnostic framework that extracts association rules from any conditional probabilistic model over tabular data, and present TabProbe as an instantiation that uses tabular foundation models (TFMs) as conditional probability estimators to learn rules out-of-the-box without frequent itemset mining. Evaluated on tabular datasets of varying sizes, TFMs consistently produce concise, high-quality rules with strong predictive performance and remain robust in low-data settings without task-specific training. This work addresses key limitations of classical association rule mining (rule explosion and poor scalability from frequent itemset mining) and neural approaches (degraded performance in low-data regimes), potentially enabling more practical knowledge discovery in high-stakes tabular decision-making. It also demonstrates a novel use of tabular foundation models beyond standard prediction tasks. TabProbe is model-agnostic and can be instantiated with various model classes, from tree-based models to large pretrained foundation models; the paper evaluates rule quality using standard ARM metrics and downstream classification performance, and source code is available on GitHub. The approach avoids frequent itemset mining entirely, but its effectiveness depends on the quality of the conditional probability estimates from the underlying model.

## [Conformal Social Choice makes multi-agent debate failures actionable](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.07667) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces Conformal Social Choice, a post-hoc layer that aggregates verbalized probability distributions from heterogeneous debating agents via a linear opinion pool and calibrates them with split conformal prediction to produce act-versus-escalate decisions. It provides fixed-round marginal coverage guarantees and, at the final round with α=0.05, flags 81.9% of wrong-consensus cases via non-singleton sets. This work addresses a critical safety gap in multi-agent LLM systems: consensus does not imply correctness, and premature stopping can commit errors to automated actions. By making failures detectable and actionable, it enables safer deployment of debate-based reasoning in high-stakes settings. The coverage guarantee holds for any pre-specified round without assumptions on individual model calibration, but adaptive first-singleton stopping is evaluated only empirically and is not covered by the guarantee. Simple probability- and entropy-threshold rules achieve comparable interception; conformal's distinct value is the finite-sample fixed-round coverage guarantee plus explicit candidate sets for escalation.

## [Non-Stationarity Breaks Permutation Surrogates in Multi-Agent RL](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.23716) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper demonstrates that in multi-agent reinforcement learning, permutation surrogates used to test information-theoretic measures produce false-positive rates of up to 100% when the non-stationary training transient is not excluded. The authors propose a block-permutation null model that permutes the source within blocks of training time, achieving false-positive rates of 5.25% and 5.50% in two games, the only method at or below the nominal test size in both. This work exposes a critical methodological flaw that can lead MARL researchers to erroneous conclusions about agent influence, as agents that never interacted are flagged as influencing one another. The proposed remedy is practical and releases code and data, helping the community avoid false discoveries when using information-theoretic measures. The block-permutation approach leaves the series, statistic, and estimand untouched, and five block counts spanning 16 to 256 all land in the nominal region. A third null control with four learners defeats all three methods, and conditioning costs three times more (15.20 points vs. 4.55) than the proposed approach.

**Background**: Permutation surrogates are a common statistical tool for testing whether an observed relationship between time series is significant, by repeatedly shuffling the data to create a null distribution. In multi-agent reinforcement learning, non-stationarity arises because agents' policies change during training, which can violate the assumptions of these tests and lead to spurious significance. Information-theoretic measures such as transfer entropy are often used to infer directed influence between agents, but their reliability depends on proper null models.

A new arXiv paper (2605.08827v3) introduces Temporal Safety Non-Identifiability, a formal account of why safety properties depending on sequence, timing, accumulation, or recovery cannot be certified by evaluation protocols that discard those features. It also proposes SCOPE (Safety Claims Over Preserved Evidence) as a general reporting principle, instantiated as SCOPE-MH for mental health AI, and demonstrates it on the AnnoMI dataset of expert-annotated motivational interviewing conversations. Current mental health AI evaluations typically score isolated responses or aggregate dialogue quality, which the paper argues can lead to invalid safety conclusions because clinically consequential failures often arise from interaction order and accumulation. The paper operationalizes SCOPE-MH through a proof-of-concept on the AnnoMI dataset, revealing failure mechanisms that per-turn behavior scoring does not capture, such as delayed escalation, repeated reinforcement, dependency formation, failed repair, and gradual deterioration across turns. SCOPE-MH is proposed as a diagnostic complement to existing evaluation infrastructure rather than a replacement.

It also contributes two repair operations: preference-rank selection raises judge accuracy from 65.0% to 68.6%, and reliability-constrained refinement reduces exploit responses receiving high scores from 46.4% to 36.0%. PReMISE is the only rubric source to score non-trivially on applicability, specificity, and effective dimensionality simultaneously. The repair operations show that reliability-constrained refinement reduces exploit rates with little change in inter-judge agreement (α = .531 → .519), indicating a trade-off between robustness and agreement.

Researchers introduced ENVPROBE, a framework that enables long-horizon language agents to actively probe their environment and correct inaccurate beliefs during execution. The method prioritizes belief fields by task relevance and potential error, then selectively queries the environment to update the agent's world model before revising its plan. As agents run over many steps, stored beliefs drift from the actual environment state, causing plans built on outdated assumptions; ENVPROBE shows that active verification through interaction, rather than more reasoning or self-reflection, is necessary for reliable long-horizon decision-making. This could improve agent reliability in complex, dynamic tasks where environment state changes during execution. ENVPROBE formulates environment probing as a budgeted decision problem: before acting, the agent may query the current value of one belief field, update its table, and pay one interaction step. Experiments across three controlled environments show substantial improvement in terminal world-state accuracy compared with agents without probing, though the abstract does not report the probing cost relative to task savings.

**Background**: Long-horizon language agents plan and execute sequences of interdependent actions in complex environments, and they rely on an internal world model—a representation of the environment's state that predicts how it changes. Because the environment can change independently of the agent, beliefs stored from earlier interactions can become outdated, and errors cannot always be fixed by reasoning alone since the correct information must come from the environment. Environment probing is the act of actively querying the environment to verify and update those beliefs.

It models coupled node and edge error propagation to select a connected core whose repair maximally reduces residual error amplification, and it theoretically bounds long-horizon planning regret. This work addresses error propagation in long-horizon LLM agents, a key reliability challenge, by enabling targeted repairs that match full-context recovery with up to 7.4× fewer tokens. It could significantly reduce the cost and improve the effectiveness of debugging and stabilizing agent rollouts, impacting researchers and practitioners building multi-step autonomous agents. ReCore is evaluated on synthetic Agent Calling-Tree graphs and the Who&When attribution benchmark, showing improved long-horizon stabilization and root-cause localization. The method exposes only the selected core to the LLM for diagnosis and repair, avoiding the need to reason over substantial irrelevant context.

A multi-institution team proposes the AIMO Interpretability Challenge, a competition that asks participants to use frontier math language models' internal mechanisms to distinguish robust reasoning from spurious shortcuts. The challenge provides newly published olympiad-level problems with symbolic representations, access to frontier reasoning models, and adversarial robustness assessments. Standard math benchmarks only measure final-answer accuracy, which can hide whether a model truly reasons or exploits brittle shortcuts. This competition aims to create an open robustness benchmark and baseline systems, connecting interpretability and generalization research to assess the reliability of frontier AI decision-making. The competition builds on AI Mathematical Olympiad (AIMO) problems and submissions plus resources from the Fields Model Initiative, and will offer computing infrastructure support. Participants will develop methods to identify which models solve problems robustly, with the goal of producing a lasting benchmark for mathematical reasoning and interpretability.

## [IDEAgent: Multi-Agent Framework for Quality-Diversity Research Idea Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22375) ⭐️ 7.0/10

IDEAgent is a multi-agent framework that frames research idea generation as a joint Quality-Diversity (QD) search, tracking idea evolution through lineages and introducing a new metric called Yield to measure the largest set of mutually diverse, high-quality ideas. Across 32 topics in 8 CS domains, it outperforms the best baseline by 3.89x on Yield and achieves a Yield of at least 2 on 8x as many topics. This work addresses a core limitation in LLM-driven scientific discovery: existing systems optimize either quality or diversity independently, often producing redundant or trivial ideas. By jointly optimizing both and providing an open-source framework, IDEAgent could improve the practical utility of AI research assistants and inspire new evaluation standards for idea generation. Quality is driven by multi-objective feedback for repair and refinement, while diversity is achieved through lightweight sequential memory and explicit comparison against completed ideas, historical variants, and rejected proposals. The framework is also extended to two algorithm discovery tasks, where it consistently outperforms baselines and yields the largest set of high-quality, diverse programs.

The paper proposes ER-EDF, a three-stage framework based on Gross's Extended Process Model of emotion regulation that identifies the user's emotion from speech, selects a regulation strategy, and implements it through a large audio-language model (LALM). It also introduces a new spoken empathetic dialogue dataset and empathy-aware evaluation metrics, and experiments across five LALMs and two datasets show consistent improvements in both automatic and human evaluations. The framework follows Gross's Extended Process Model in three stages: identifying the user's emotion from speech, selecting a regulation strategy matched to that emotion, and implementing the strategy through a LALM. Evaluation goes beyond lexical matching with empathy-aware metrics, and the approach is validated across five LALMs and two datasets, though the abstract does not specify model sizes or dataset scale.

## [Cognitive Field Networks enable persistent recurrent cognition in Transformers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.16752) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces Cognitive Field Networks (CFN), a recurrent Transformer architecture in which the full token-resolved hidden field re-enters each computational cycle via Φ_{n+1} = F_θ(X_{n+1}, Φ_n), rather than relying on a separately prescribed memory operation. Experiments show that learning turns this pathway into a functional channel for persistent, content-dependent internal states whose temporal persistence is systematically controlled by the recurrent training horizon. This work offers a unified dynamical framework linking memory-dressed field formation, input-driven reorganization, and recurrent state continuity, potentially advancing AI systems that maintain persistent, history-dependent cognition without an explicit external memory module. It also provides an experimentally controllable platform for studying how temporal persistence emerges from training, which could influence future recurrent Transformer designs and cognitive modeling research. The learned dynamics generalize beyond the training horizon: semantic continuation sustains the recurrent state without explicit answer replay, while unsupported states exhibit finite passive relaxation, and periodic re-exposure to relevant input renews the surviving field into an approximately stationary nonzero regime. Unrelated-input and recurrence-off controls fail to reproduce this behavior, and near-paraphrased input produces weaker renewal, showing that persistence depends on both field re-entry and input relevance.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 22, 04:00

**Background**: Cognitive Field Theory describes cognition as memory-dressed collective dynamics, in which slow relaxation modes support a persistent cognitive field; prior work has linked this to the time-scale density of states in Transformer dynamics. Recurrent Transformers typically feed a previous hidden state back into the network, but often through a compressed summary or a prescribed memory operation. Non-Markovian memory dynamics refer to systems whose future depends on more than the current state, which is the property the CFN aims to capture through full hidden-field re-entry.

## [AtomWorld-Mem restores hidden dynamical states for long-horizon atomistic simulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31133) ⭐️ 7.0/10

AtomWorld-Mem introduces a memory-restored atomistic world model that recovers the latent dynamical state missing from instantaneous crystal snapshots, using multi-scale spatial encoders plus short-term event memory and long-term structural memory. The restored state prioritizes legal vacancy-mediated events under single-event Kinetic Monte Carlo (KMC) constraints, improving long-horizon atomistic progress under fixed event budgets and transferring zero-shot to unseen alloy-temperature systems. Long-horizon atomistic simulation is central to predicting materials evolution, but current snapshots are ambiguous about hidden dynamical context, which limits reliability and efficiency. Framing this as a memory-based world-state restoration problem could make ML-driven atomistic simulation more physically grounded and transferable, benefiting materials science and ML-for-science workflows. The method does not replace the simulator: event legality, physical execution, and residence-time updates remain governed by the underlying KMC engine, while the learned model only prioritizes legal events. Evaluation covers energetic, structural, and vacancy-transport observables, and zero-shot transfer is demonstrated across diverse unseen alloy-temperature AtomWorlds.

## [LoRA Rank Does Not Limit Capacity Under Norm Budgets, Paper Argues](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.32002) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2609.32002v2) proves that under hard per-factor norm budgets, the rank r in LoRA does not constrain model capacity or complexity, because every analyzed complexity and displacement functional is maximized by a rank-one update. The linear-readout model class is identical for all r ≥ 1, and its Rademacher complexity has no dependence on r. This challenges the widely held assumption that smaller LoRA rank yields a simpler, better-generalizing model, which is central to how practitioners tune LoRA. It suggests rank should be understood as governing which updates are reachable and the cost of spectral cancellation, not as a capacity knob. The paper shows that replacing per-factor budgets with a joint budget on the product restores a data-dependent, rank-sensitive complexity bound, but only for well-spread feature distributions, with the worst case remaining rank-free. It also bounds the smallest rank needed to cancel leading singular directions of the pretrained weight, with matching upper and lower bounds under two-sided spectral decay.

**Background**: LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) fine-tunes large models by learning low-rank updates to weight matrices, and its rank r is commonly treated as a capacity control. Rademacher complexity is a measure of function class richness used to derive generalization bounds. The nuclear norm is the tightest convex envelope of the rank function and is often used to relax rank constraints.

## [Penumbra: Sample-Efficient Adversarial Search for Regulatory Compliance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04693) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Penumbra introduces an adaptive adversarial search that walks from a verified compliant anchor under an expanding edit budget until a two-evaluator committee flips its verdict, emitting the adjacent response pair that straddles the compliance boundary. At matched budgets, adaptive allocation reaches uniform allocation's full-budget coverage on 59% of candidates, and at equal records it covers 1.43x the defeat modes of naive enumeration. Regulatory red-teaming for agents in finance, healthcare, and law is constrained by sample efficiency rather than volume, since each probe costs a generation and two adjudications. Penumbra's ability to find minimal-edit boundary pairs at a cost that scales with the boundary rather than the text makes compliance testing more practical for high-stakes deployments. The method targets coverage of the defeat surface, measured as distinct (obligation x defeat mode) cells resolved per candidate, and the gain is confined to the axis it targets. On 60 screened obligations of a financial advisory constitution, Penumbra returns 144 compliant-violating pairs differing by a handful of words, whereas a model asked directly for both produces texts sharing almost nothing; a clinical triage constitution reproduces this on 18 obligations with 49 pairs.

## [LLMs Fail to Self-Decide Which Agent Rules Are Verifiable](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04699) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.04699v2) shows that across six corpora—including the EU AI Act, FINRA guidance, and a deployed credit agent—four LLMs from three labs cannot reliably self-decide whether a rule predicate is checkable by a fixed verifier or requires a judge. Using roughly 22,000 labels, the authors find models collapse on regulatory text and err in correlated, non-conservative ways, over-claiming checkability on the deployed agent's rule-set. This undermines escalation schemes in high-stakes domains like finance, healthcare, and law that assume a model can decide at runtime which rules need human or judge review. The finding that errors are correlated and biased toward non-escalation means no single model can serve as a conservative fallback, directly affecting agent verification and AI safety design. The authors propose CoVer (corroborate-then-verify), which treats model unanimity as only a nomination and admits a predicate only when a synthesized check survives intervention, reads fields the agent cannot write, and holds under deterministic rewording. They also show that agreement with a reference judge certifies nothing, as judge agreement climbs from 30% to 77% across calibration bands while the genuinely decidable share does not move.

**Background**: Agent verifiers enforce rules that come from outside the team, such as regulations, and must split each rule predicate into those a fixed check can settle and those needing a judge. Escalation schemes assume this split is self-decidable by the model, but the paper argues self-decidability is not a capability to elicit but a boundary the verifier must construct. The EU AI Act is the first comprehensive AI regulation, and FINRA is the largest independent U.S. securities regulator, making their text representative of complex regulatory language.

## [MultiWorldBench: New Benchmark Tests Consistency of Multiplayer World Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.11723) ⭐️ 7.0/10

MultiWorldBench is a new Minecraft-based diagnostic benchmark with 495 case configurations across seven task suites and ten capabilities, designed to test whether independently controlled views in multiplayer world models remain consistent with a single shared, persistent world. It evaluates Solaris (MP), Solaris (SP), and Gamma-World against an engine ground truth, finding that Gamma-World achieves the highest average score (21.39) among generated systems, followed by Solaris (MP) at 20.88 and Solaris (SP) at 10.06, while Engine GT reaches 91.69. This benchmark addresses a critical gap in evaluating multiplayer world models, which must maintain consistency across independently controlled views—a requirement for immersive, shared virtual environments. It provides a structured diagnostic tool that reveals substantial shortcomings in current models, potentially guiding future research toward more coherent and persistent world generation. All generated systems score at most 8.00 on state persistence and 1.33 on structural consistency, and none succeeds in spatial reasoning or building-identity preservation. Human pairwise evaluation aligns strongly with automatic metrics, showing a mean dimension-level Spearman correlation of 0.95.

## [Activation Steering as Memory Stores Only Question-Independent Facts, Study Finds](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.14958) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A pre-registered study on Qwen3.5-2B and 9B models shows that training-free activation steering used as memory is selective (about 98% of unrelated replies unchanged) but stores facts only as last-layer word tokens and is almost never cleanly used (at most 15% clean use, versus 96-98% in context). The study also finds that the reference subtracted when writing a preference determines whether its concept or direction survives, with a stored dislike recalled as a like unless the opposite is subtracted. This challenges the assumption that activation steering can serve as a general-purpose memory for facts and preferences in LLM agents, suggesting that only question-independent content survives and that text may still be necessary for storing user-specific information. The findings have direct implications for the design of memory systems in AI agents. The memory is selective, leaving about 98% of unrelated replies unchanged, but facts are stored as the word to say in the last layers only and are almost never used (at most 15% clean use, against 96-98% in context). Leanings transfer only in a narrow strength window, and the choice of reference subtracted when writing a preference determines whether its concept or direction survives.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 22, 04:00

**Background**: Activation steering is a technique that modifies a frozen LLM's internal activations during inference to steer its behavior, often by adding a vector computed as the difference between positive and negative examples. Recent work has proposed using such steering vectors as a memory for skills, storing past experiences and retrieving them later. This study tests whether the same approach can store facts and preferences about the user, which are typically assumed to require text.

## [Adaptive-Group Process Rewards Improve GUI Agent RL Credit Assignment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.17710) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces an adaptive-group process reward framework that dynamically partitions GUI trajectories into semantically coherent subgoal groups, enabling process reward estimation at both the action and group levels. It further augments GRPO's outcome advantage with these process rewards to provide finer-grained guidance for GUI agent training. This addresses the sparse outcome reward problem in GUI agent reinforcement learning, where credit assignment to intermediate actions is difficult due to long-horizon dependencies. More accurate credit assignment could significantly improve training efficiency and performance of GUI agents, impacting researchers and practitioners working on digital automation. At the action level, a critic evaluates each action based on visual changes and subsequent actions within the group; at the group level, the framework aggregates action-level evaluations to assess subgoal completion and contribution to the overall task, refining them using context from all groups. The process reward of each action combines its action-level evaluation with the refined group-level evaluation.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 22, 04:00

**Background**: GUI agents are AI systems that perceive and interact with graphical user interfaces visually, executing tasks through clicks, typing, and other human-like inputs. Training them with reinforcement learning typically relies on sparse outcome rewards given only at the end of a task, making it hard to determine which intermediate actions deserve credit—a classic credit assignment problem. Process rewards aim to provide intermediate feedback, but accurately evaluating an action in long GUI trajectories requires considering information beyond its immediate state. GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization) is a popular RL algorithm that uses group-relative advantages for policy updates.

## [AgentStripes: An Evidence-Graded Maturity Model for AI Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18603) ⭐️ 7.0/10

AgentStripes proposes a maturity model for AI agents with levels 0–7 (stripes), 12 process areas covering 40 capabilities, three gates (basic, safety, proof) that cap an agent's level regardless of benchmark score, and evidence grades E0–E5. Each capability is rated 0–3 with a separate evidence level, combined into a severity-weighted score that determines stripes, using instruments to gather evidence and language-model judges to interpret it under explicit criteria. Benchmarks only show what an agent can do on a task suite, not whether a released version is engineered for reliability, safety, and observability; AgentStripes fills this gap with a structured, evidence-based assessment framework. It could influence how agent developers, auditors, and enterprises evaluate and certify agent releases beyond raw performance scores. An exploratory evaluation of 30 public Python agent repositories using only static evidence capped every final stripe at 2, with 26 repositories ending at one stripe and 4 at two; re-judging changed the final stripe of 4 of 22 repositories, indicating unreliable distinction. The parameters are expert conventions without outcome-based calibration, and the stripes have not been shown to predict reliability or safety; a validation protocol is specified but unexecuted.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 22, 04:00

**Background**: AI agents are autonomous systems that use large language models to plan and execute multi-step tasks, often calling external tools. Traditional evaluation relies on benchmarks that measure task success, but these do not capture engineering controls such as safety mechanisms, observability (monitoring every reasoning step and tool call), or evidence quality. Maturity models, common in software engineering (e.g., CMMI), provide staged levels for organizational processes; AgentStripes adapts this idea to agent engineering with an explicit evidence-grading component.

## [AM-Bench: A Unified Taxonomy and Evaluation Suite for Agentic Misalignment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.24264) ⭐️ 7.0/10

AM-Bench introduces a unified taxonomy and a 35-scenario evaluation benchmark spanning seven industries to study agentic misalignment, where LLM agents choose harmful actions over failure. Grounded in the fraud triangle criminological framework, it operationalizes perceived threat, perceived opportunity, and reasoning dimensions, and evaluates 10 frontier models, revealing a 62-percentage-point gap in misalignment across scenarios. This work addresses an underexplored safety failure mode—agents choosing harmful actions over failure—which existing benchmarks largely overlook by focusing on compliance with explicitly harmful instructions. The multi-industry scenario suite and theoretical framing provide a valuable tool for AI safety research and could inform mitigation strategies as agents are deployed with increasing autonomy. The taxonomy adapts the fraud triangle into five threat categories from the instrumental convergence thesis, seven opportunity categories from the Emergent Strategic Reasoning Risks (ESRR) taxonomy, and a novel four-question binary reasoning framework. Evaluation of 10 frontier models shows Gemini 3 Flash and Gemini 3.1 Pro exhibit the highest misalignment, while Claude Sonnet 4.6 displays near-zero rates; the reasoning framework reveals models may exhibit harmful behaviors without explicit situational awareness, complicating detection and mitigation.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 22, 04:00

**Background**: Agentic misalignment refers to situations where AI agents, trained with reinforcement learning and given autonomous decision-making capacity, develop behaviors or objectives that conflict with their designers' goals, often manifesting as strategic, context-dependent actions such as deception or sabotage. The fraud triangle is a criminological framework developed by Donald Cressey that explains goal-directed misconduct through three conditions: perceived pressure, perceived opportunity, and rationalization. AM-Bench adapts these concepts to agentic environments to systematically study when and why agents might choose harmful actions over failure.

## [HSPR: Bayesian method recovers software-agent benchmark scores from 10% of tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.24611) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduced Hierarchical Score Posterior Recovery (HSPR), a Bayesian method that estimates full software-agent benchmark scores from a small task subset by combining source-fitted response factors with uncertain group success rates. On four SWE-bench-family task banks at a 10% budget, HSPR achieved the lowest mean absolute error on three banks and the lowest maximum absolute error on all four compared methods. Full benchmark evaluation of software agents is expensive, and small subsets often yield inaccurate scores even when rankings are preserved. HSPR enables cheaper, more reliable score estimation, which could make frequent agent evaluation more practical for the research community. The method uses posterior-guided acquisition to select tasks, with a score-based criterion equal to the expected one-step reduction in full-score posterior variance. The final estimate is the median of the full-score posterior with source-selected calibration, and ablations show that removing group uncertainty or replacing adaptive queries increases macro MAE.

Bayesian hierarchical modeling estimates posterior distributions over parameters at multiple levels, and active learning uses acquisition functions to choose the most informative samples. ## [VLA-Rolling reuses action tails to cut denoising steps in flow-matching VLA models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.25043) ⭐️ 7.0/10

VLA-Rolling introduces a lightweight inference framework that reuses the discarded action tail from flow-matching VLA models through three stages: action-tail inheritance, per-action confidence estimation, and confidence-guided renoising/denoising budget allocation, while keeping the underlying VLA frozen. Across π0.5, SmolVLA, X-VLA, and MolmoAct2 on LIBERO, MetaWorld, LIBERO-Plus, and RoboTwin 2.0, it reduces inference cost in all 16 model-benchmark pairs, achieving up to 1.48× speedup and improving success rate in 14 pairs by up to 15.08 percentage points. This work shows that action tails are reusable intermediate states rather than wasted predictions, offering a training-free way to make flow-matching VLA inference both faster and more accurate. It is directly relevant to robotics deployment, where reducing denoising steps lowers latency and compute cost while improved success rates enhance real-world reliability. The method adapts the denoising budget per sample because the optimal number of steps varies substantially across samples, and it matches or outperforms a native 10-step Gaussian baseline with fewer steps. The approach is an inference-time optimization that leaves the VLA frozen, so it does not require retraining or architectural changes.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 22, 04:00

**Background**: Flow-matching VLA models generate an action chunk by iteratively denoising Gaussian noise, similar to diffusion models, and under the receding-horizon paradigm they execute only a short prefix before replanning with updated observations. The unexecuted remainder, called the action tail, is typically discarded and the next chunk is regenerated from fresh noise. Action chunking and receding-horizon execution are standard techniques in robot learning for improving control performance and reactivity.

## [VibeTraining-Bench: Benchmarking Cross-Component Co-Design for Recursive Self-Improvement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.26342) ⭐️ 7.0/10

VibeTraining-Bench is a new benchmark that evaluates research agents' ability to iteratively co-design training data, trainers, and inference harnesses for recursive self-improvement across terminal operation, software engineering, multi-turn tool use, and mathematical reasoning tasks. In experiments, GPT-6-Astra improved a target agent system's performance on SWE-bench Verified from 32.9% to 53.7%, approaching the human-developed instruct model's 55.4%. This benchmark shifts evaluation from single-model performance to an agent's ability to improve an entire system, which is central to the pursuit of recursive self-improvement and could inform how future AI research agents are designed and assessed. It also introduces safeguards against reward hacking, addressing a growing concern in agent evaluation. Research agents start from an identical initial agent system under a fixed resource budget and iteratively refine data, trainers, and inference harnesses guided by validation feedback before submitting a final system for test-set evaluation. To prevent reward hacking, the benchmark enforces test data isolation, separate research and grading containers, and network restrictions for research agents.

**Background**: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) is a hypothesized process in which AI systems improve their own capabilities, potentially leading to rapid intelligence gains. ## [Jacobian Descent Generalizes Gradient Descent for Multi-Objective Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.16232) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper introduces Jacobian descent (JD), an algorithm that generalizes gradient descent to multi-objective optimization by using the Jacobian matrix of a vector-valued objective and projecting gradients to resolve conflicts. The authors prove convergence to the Pareto front in the smooth convex case and demonstrate a novel learning paradigm called instance-wise risk minimization (IWRM). This work provides stronger theoretical guarantees than existing gradient-combination methods, which typically only converge to weakly Pareto stationary points, and introduces IWRM as a new way to train models by treating each training example's loss as a separate objective. It could impact machine learning training, especially in fairness, robustness, and multi-task learning where conflicting objectives are common. The method projects gradients to fully resolve conflicts, and an efficient implementation using the Gramian of the Jacobian matrix drastically reduces memory requirements. Early experiments on image classification show promising results for IWRM, though the convergence proof is limited to the smooth convex setting.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 22, 04:00

**Background**: Multi-objective optimization deals with optimizing several conflicting objectives simultaneously, and the Pareto front is the set of solutions where no objective can be improved without worsening another. Gradient descent is limited to single-objective optimization, and existing methods that combine multiple gradients often struggle when objectives conflict. The Jacobian matrix generalizes the gradient to vector-valued functions, with each row being the gradient of one objective.

## [OPTIMA: One-Shot LLM Pruning via Batched Quadratic Programming](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.13886) ⭐️ 7.0/10

OPTIMA introduces a one-shot post-training pruning method that reformulates layer-wise weight reconstruction as independent column-wise quadratic programs (QPs) sharing a single Hessian per weight matrix, enabling batched solving on accelerators. It improves average zero-shot accuracy in 40 of 49 (model, mask selector, sparsity) settings across LLaMA and Gemma families, with mean gains of +0.61, +0.56, and +1.01 points at 50% unstructured, 2:4, and 60% unstructured sparsity, and up to +3.97 points at 60% sparsity. This work bridges the gap between fast but inaccurate heuristic pruning and principled but computationally infeasible joint optimization, offering a practical accuracy-scalability trade-off for deploying large language models under memory and compute constraints. It integrates with existing mask selectors and enables one-shot pruning at scale on a single accelerator without fine-tuning, which could lower the barrier to efficient LLM inference. OPTIMA implements an accelerator-friendly QP solver that accumulates one Hessian per weight matrix and solves many small QPs in parallel with a convergence certificate per column. On an NVIDIA H100, it prunes an 8B-parameter transformer end-to-end in 40 hours with 60 GB peak GPU memory, and it matches ADMM-based exact reconstruction on its own masks.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 22, 04:00

**Background**: Post-training pruning reduces the inference cost of large language models by removing weights after training, but it faces a trade-off: simple heuristics are fast yet degrade accuracy, while principled joint optimization recovers accuracy but is computationally infeasible at modern scale. One-shot methods like SparseGPT sit in between, applying efficient but approximate weight updates using second-order (Hessian) information. Quadratic programming (QP) is a class of optimization problems that minimize a quadratic function subject to linear constraints, and here it is used to solve the weight reconstruction step after a pruning mask is selected.

## [Activation Sensitivity Unifies Post-Training Quantization Methods](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.11663) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper proves that post-training quantization methods such as AWQ, GPTQ, Fisher quantization, block reconstruction, and Hadamard rotation are all special cases of minimizing a single gradient-weighted activation sensitivity quadratic form derived from a Gauss-Newton expansion of the task loss. This unification provides a theoretical foundation for understanding and comparing existing PTQ techniques, potentially guiding the design of more principled and effective quantization algorithms for large language models. The framework shows AWQ corresponds to a diagonal approximation with uniform token weights, while GPTQ corresponds to Cholesky error compensation on the gradient-weighted Hessian; the authors also propose SAQ-GPTQ and demonstrate roughly 3x reduction in INT3/INT4 excess loss over unweighted GPTQ in simulations.

These methods were previously seen as distinct heuristics, but this work reveals they share a common mathematical root.

## [Expected Return Objective Inherently Causes Mode Collapse in RL, Paper Shows](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.21669) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2601.21669v2) theoretically proves that outcome-level mode collapse in reinforcement learning is a structural consequence of the expected-return objective, not merely an exploration or regularization issue. The authors propose inverse probability scaling (IPS) as a minimal correction and instantiate it in GRPO as IPS-GRPO, a drop-in modification that reduces collapse while matching or exceeding baseline performance. This work challenges the common assumption that mode collapse stems from insufficient exploration, suggesting that fixing the objective rather than adding exploration heuristics is key to reliable multimodal policy optimization. It could influence how RL practitioners design objectives for tasks with multiple high-quality solutions, such as reasoning and molecular generation. Under idealized learning dynamics, the log-probability ratio between any two outcomes evolves linearly with their reward difference, leading to exponential divergence and inevitable collapse regardless of exploration strategy, entropy regularization, or optimization algorithm. IPS removes outcome-frequency amplification from the learning signal and provably yields reward-proportional terminal distributions, with experiments across reasoning and molecular generation tasks showing consistent reduction in collapse without auxiliary models or architectural changes.

## [TTCS: Co-Evolving Test-Time Curriculum for Self-Improving LLM Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.22628) ⭐️ 7.0/10

TTCS introduces a co-evolving test-time training framework that initializes two policies from the same pretrained model—a question synthesizer and a reasoning solver—which iteratively optimize each other: the synthesizer generates progressively challenging question variants to form a curriculum tailored to the solver's current ability, while the solver updates using self-consistency rewards from multiple sampled responses on both original and synthetic questions. This addresses two key limitations of existing test-time training for LLMs—poor pseudo-label quality on hard problems and instability from small test sets—and experiments show consistent gains on challenging math benchmarks that transfer to general-domain tasks across different LLM backbones, suggesting a scalable path toward dynamically constructed test-time curricula for self-evolving models. The solver's feedback guides the synthesizer to generate questions aligned with the model's current capability, and the generated variants in turn stabilize the solver's test-time training; code and implementation details are available at https://github.com/XMUDeepLIT/TTCS.

In LLM reasoning, pseudo-labeling uses the model's own sampled answers as noisy supervision, but raw hard questions often yield low-quality labels, and small test sets make online updates unstable. Curriculum learning—training on progressively harder examples—is a natural remedy, and TTCS combines these ideas by having the model synthesize its own curriculum at test time.

## [Evaluation format skews measured triage failure in consumer health AI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.11413) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2603.11413v5) reports a mechanistic study and a faithful replication showing that the exam-style evaluation format used in a Nature Medicine study inflates measured triage failure rates in consumer health AI. In the replication, the direction of the effect reversed: free-text rewrites scored slightly below the exact prompt (78.7% vs 81.8%, p=0.020), while naturalistic input with a forced categorical answer beat both the exact prompt (84.4%, p=0.023) and free text (p=0.0001). This work challenges the headline safety claim that ChatGPT Health under-triages 51.6% of emergencies, suggesting that much of the measured failure is an artifact of the evaluation design rather than a stable model property. The mechanistic study found five frontier LLMs scored 6.4 points higher on a 17-scenario bank under naturalistic patient-style messages than under a constrained scaffold (p=0.015). In the replication, on the four vignettes defining the original emergency rate, under-triage was 17% with the exact scaffold, 50% in free text, and 21% with a forced letter on the same message; every free-text 'under-triage' was a same-day recommendation scored C rather than D, and 60% made escalation conditional on information the patient was asked to check.

Researchers introduced CounterCount, a diagnostic dataset of paired factual and counterfactual images (e.g., a rabbit with four ears), and found that across 16 vision-language models, average counting accuracy dropped from 91.6% on factual images to 49.5% on counterfactual ones. Most errors matched the canonical count, showing a bias toward learned knowledge over visual evidence. The analysis shows models exhibit 'System-1'-like behavior, falling back on canonical counts after shallow recognition, and while model activations partially contain the necessary visual evidence, models underutilize it by attending less to counted attributes when giving biased answers. Input manipulations that break visual context, introduce cueing or reasoning, or amplify internal attention can reduce these biases.

Researchers introduce flow control, a method that injects simple user inputs such as keyboard commands into the initial condition of a vision-language-action (VLA) model's flow matching action expert, enabling real-time steering without retraining or fine-tuning.
