It also shows that fine-tuning on flow control trajectories can improve the autonomous policy itself, bridging human intervention and autonomous learning. Flow control is robust to suboptimal user inputs and enables users to achieve significantly higher success rates and faster task completion; additionally, fine-tuning a VLA on flow control trajectories improves the autonomous policy. Many recent VLAs use flow matching, a generative modeling technique that learns a deterministic vector field to transform noise into actions via numerical integration. For heterogeneous workloads, the authors prove a stability criterion in the two-class common-input setting and show that coprime decoding lengths can stabilize the eviction-free equilibrium. This work identifies service-induced congestion as a structural instability mechanism in LLM serving, where the service process itself creates future capacity pressure, leading to evictions and wasted computation. The derived scheduling design principles, such as using coprime decoding lengths, could help systems researchers and practitioners sustain high throughput in memory-constrained serving environments. The model captures admission, memory growth, and eviction under continuous batching, and shows that except for a Lebesgue-measure-zero exact-capture set, the system converges to a unique asymptotically stable limit cycle. Under an input-dominated scaling regime, coprime decoding lengths stabilize the eviction-free equilibrium, while non-coprime lengths create synchronized modes that drive instability.

**Background**: In LLM serving, each request accumulates GPU memory as its key-value (KV) cache grows with every generated token. Continuous batching improves throughput by dynamically adding and removing requests, but under high concurrency, aggregate memory usage increases endogenously over time. When memory capacity is exceeded, systems evict active requests, discarding cached state and restarting them later, which wastes computation. The interaction intent is represented through learned contact patterns and shared across morphologically different robots, while the kinematic decoder is trained purely on synthetic data generated from each embodiment's kinematic model. ## [Bounded DiD on LLM Judge Ratings Can Manufacture Spurious Effects](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.27309) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2608.27309v4) proves in closed form that difference-in-differences (DiD) on a bounded rating scale can produce a spurious interaction effect when a common severity shift is attenuated unequally by the scale bounds. In a pre-registered audit of 990 calls to a frozen pedagogy LLM judge, the registered primary analysis found no effect of a stated novice or advanced profile on scaffolding preference, while the only nominally significant secondary interaction (+0.378 points, p=0.002) on productive struggle was reproduced at 79–85% by a post-hoc construction with zero differential preference, using only the observed severity shift and the scale floor. This matters for the growing body of LLM-as-judge evaluation work, where DiD designs are increasingly used to audit judge bias, and for applied econometrics more broadly, because it shows that a nominally significant interaction on a bounded scale may not identify differential preference on the latent scale. Researchers relying on such audits could draw false conclusions about judge bias unless they account for bound-induced attenuation. The paper builds on prior work on nonlinear difference-in-differences and shows the problem in closed form; the empirical demonstration uses a pre-registered audit of 990 calls to a frozen pedagogy judge, with the primary analysis null and only a secondary productive-struggle interaction reaching nominal significance. A post-hoc construction with zero differential preference reproduced 79–85% of that interaction using the observed severity shift and the scale floor alone, implying the observed interaction does not identify differential preference on the latent scale.

**Background**: Difference-in-differences is a widely used causal-inference design that compares changes over time or across conditions between treated and control groups. When ratings are bounded, a shift common to both responses can be compressed unevenly near the floor or ceiling, so an apparent interaction can arise even without any true differential preference.

## [OPIS: A New Input-Grounded Benchmark for Multi-Object Memory in Video World Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.35052) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduced OPIS, an input-grounded benchmark that evaluates multi-object memory in video world models by anchoring assessment to a fixed set of object instances from the initial observation. The dataset contains 500 cases across real-world, embodied-robotic, and game-world domains, with dense object-level annotations for 12,672 rigid, articulated, and deformable instances, and a hierarchical evaluator measuring Object Presence, Identity, and Structure. Existing evaluation protocols often rely on generated histories, video references, or selected revisit viewpoints, which can confound the measurement of a model's true memory capability. OPIS addresses this confound and provides a standardized, object-centric way to compare world models, which matters for researchers building video generation and world simulation systems that must maintain persistent scene state. Across eight image-to-video or camera-conditioned world models, OPIS scores range from 48.65 to 56.01, and as the reference inventory grows from fewer than 20 to more than 40 objects, the average Identity score falls from 40.22 to 23.11. The evaluator combines association and explicit visibility reasoning, using static or dynamic tracks based on object kinematics, and the results show that preserving particular input object instances is considerably harder than generating plausible visual elements.

A key requirement for such models is temporal coherence and long-range memory, so that objects and scene state persist over time. Object-centric memory approaches, such as persistent 3D object memories or slot-based KV memory, have emerged to reduce identity drift when entities leave and re-enter the frame. OPIS contributes a benchmark specifically designed to measure whether models preserve the exact object instances given in the input, rather than merely producing visually plausible content.

## [UMM-Reflection: Interleaved RL Enables Self-Repair in Unified Multimodal Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.35767) ⭐️ 7.0/10

UMM-Reflection introduces interleaved reinforcement learning over complete reflection trajectories to jointly train reflection text and image revisions in unified multimodal models, enabling self-repair of generated images. On BAGEL, it improves GenEval by 12.05 points over SFT, with gains transferring to WISE (+10.97), OneIG-Bench (+3.48), and T2I-CompBench++ (+4.63), none of which are used in training. This work addresses a real limitation of supervised fine-tuning and naive RL for self-reflection in image generation, showing that trajectory-level credit assignment across both reflection and rendering can yield substantial and transferable improvements. It could influence how unified multimodal models are trained for iterative self-correction, reducing reliance on external critics or verifiers at inference. Sibling trajectories share one initial image so that group-relative advantage compares reflection strategies, and a single trajectory-level advantage updates both reflection tokens and flow-based revisions, avoiding combinatorial blow-up of per-round credit assignment. No verifier is needed at inference, and credit flows across rounds to both roles of the same model.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 22, 04:00

**Background**: Unified multimodal models combine understanding and generation in a single architecture, so they can in principle inspect and revise their own outputs. However, whether a revision helps is only known after rendering, making it hard to train reflection and generation jointly. Reinforcement learning with group-relative advantages (e.g., GRPO-style) compares multiple sampled trajectories to estimate which strategies are better, and flow-based image generation produces images by integrating a learned velocity field.

## [Binarization Flattens the Score Space](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.35797) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2609.35797v2) shows that collapsing LLM judge scores to pass/fail ({0,1}) hides affine stretches of the underlying score scale, and proposes a three-grade scheme (e.g., {0, 0.5, 1}) that removes this ambiguity. On MATH and SciBench outputs from a seven-criterion judge, all 14 constructed criterionwise stretches were invisible after binarization but visible with three grades. This matters because LLM judges are widely used as rewards in post-training, and binarizing their scores can let policies exploit invisible score-scale changes without affecting reported verdicts. The finding affects reward modeling and evaluation research, suggesting that keeping at least three grades closes one blind spot. Under a joint-Gaussian model, a third grade adds a second threshold and removes the affine stretch ambiguity; at n=1,024, a test given both population laws had at least 96.5% power at a 1.5× stress. However, verdicts alone remain insufficient because arbitrary within-grade changes and fixed-covariance, loading-aligned mean shifts (a sycophancy-shaped lift) are still indistinguishable from genuine improvement, and the shared-factor reference approximation fit MATH and SciBench but not HealthBench.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 22, 04:00

**Background**: LLM judges are language models prompted to score other model outputs, often used as rewards when deterministic verifiers cannot capture an objective. Binarization reduces these scores to pass/fail, which is simple but discards information about how well each criterion was met. The paper models each verdict as a score on an unreported scale compared against a cutoff, so proportional stretches of that scale never change the verdict.

## [BreakingWeb Benchmark Makes Browser-Agent Tasks Harder via Controlled Interventions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.35814) ⭐️ 7.0/10

BreakingWeb introduces a benchmark that runs each browser-use task twice: once on an unmodified self-hosted website and once under a controlled, reproducible intervention to the site's content, server state, network responses, or rendered page, while keeping the instruction and success criterion fixed. It contains 519 task pairs across seven self-hosted websites and scores each run against the website's final backend state. Rather than collecting costly new tasks and websites, BreakingWeb makes difficulty a programmable property of the environment, offering a cheaper and more diagnostic way to evaluate browser-use agents. Its results show that six strong agents lose 22.9 percentage points on average under interventions, with 75% of failures being belief failures where the agent wrongly declares success, which highlights a key reliability gap for web automation. Each intervention is designed to be detectable and recoverable by a competent human and is labeled with the behavior recovery mainly requires, such as verification. Humans' pass rates drop only 10.0 points on the first attempt and 5.7 points when repeating the task, and the benchmark also evaluates three screenshot-only agents alongside the six browser-use agents.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 22, 04:00

**Background**: Browser-use agents are LLM-driven systems that operate a real browser, reading pages and deciding what to click or type to complete a task, unlike scrapers that rely on hand-written selectors. As these agents improve, benchmarks have grown by adding new tasks, websites, and applications, but this is costly and makes it unclear which factors drive difficulty. BreakingWeb instead exploits the modular structure of web environments—server logic, network responses, and client-side interfaces—to inject interventions at different layers while preserving task semantics and realism.

Researchers introduce ROSS (Relearning from Self-Generated Rollouts through Selective Supervision), which keeps full historical rollout trajectories as context but applies loss only to selected model-generated continuations. The method shows that self-generated rollouts contain reusable behavioral experience that can be exploited through offline supervised fine-tuning without additional policy rollouts, potentially lowering the cost of post-training. It consistently improves upstream checkpoints across domain-specific RL, multi-teacher on-policy distillation, and agentic RL, affecting teams working on math, code, instruction following, and software engineering. ROSS disentangles trajectory filtering from token-level selective supervision, comparing positive-rollout SFT, ROSS without masking, and full ROSS. The approach targets mistakes, abandoned attempts, and redundant actions in historical rollouts that should not be imitated, while preserving behaviors the current policy no longer expresses reliably.

## [S^3: Spectral Null-Space Swap Makes Reasoning Models Efficient](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.37976) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper proposes Spectral Null-Space Swap (S^3), a training-free method that composes Non-thinking and Thinking model checkpoints by keeping the Non-thinking model's dominant subspace and taking the Thinking checkpoint's component outside it (the null space). Across 2B-30B dense and MoE models in 28 environments, S^3 reduces inference token overhead by an average of 27.4% versus full Thinking models while improving overall accuracy by 1.0 percentage point. Chain-of-thought reasoning models achieve strong accuracy but incur excessive token costs, and S^3 offers a training-free way to cut that overhead without sacrificing the gains from thinking-mode post-training. This could make reasoning models cheaper to deploy across mathematical, multimodal, and audio domains, and it introduces null-space analysis as a new lens for model optimization beyond the dominant subspace. The method is evaluated on 2B-30B dense and mixture-of-experts architectures across 28 environments, achieving for example +8.3% accuracy on HMMT25 with a 33.0% token speedup. The authors explain the effect via attention entropy, showing that the retained component yields more concentrated attention, and support it with a simplified analytical optimization model; however, the work is currently available only as an abstract, so full implementation and reproducibility details are not yet public.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 22, 04:00

**Background**: Chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting and post-training encourage LLMs to generate intermediate reasoning steps, which improves accuracy but greatly increases the number of tokens generated and thus inference cost. Singular value decomposition (SVD) factorizes a matrix into orthogonal components ordered by singular values, where the largest singular values define the dominant directions and the null space consists of vectors mapped to zero. This paper finds that the reasoning ability gained during thinking-mode post-training resides largely in the Thinking model's weight component within the null space of the Non-thinking model's dominant singular directions.

## [StepRS-GRPO: Stepwise Risk-Sensitive RL Boosts Diffusion Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00661) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces StepRS-GRPO, a reinforcement learning method that varies the risk coefficient of the group-advantage transformation across denoising states in diffusion large language models (dLLMs). Experiments across multiple dLLM backbones and mathematical reasoning benchmarks show improvements in both pass@1 accuracy and pass@k coverage over centered GRPO, along with increased answer diversity. This work addresses a key inefficiency in applying reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) to dLLMs, where terminal feedback is reused across changing denoising contexts. By improving reasoning performance and diversity, it could advance the development of diffusion-based language models as alternatives to autoregressive models for complex reasoning tasks. For binary rewards, the transformation is exactly a prompt- and state-dependent rescaling of centered outcome advantages, and a capability-based calibration suggests a coefficient scale. Ablation studies with mass-matched controls and RMS matching of advantages support the contributions of state allocation and schedule direction, and reasoning-trace diagnostics show diversity gains extend beyond final-answer strings.

## [EDISCO: First Exactly E(2)-Equivariant Discrete Diffusion Model for Euclidean Combinatorial Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04953) ⭐️ 7.0/10

EDISCO introduces the first discrete diffusion model for Euclidean combinatorial optimization problems (ECOPs) that achieves exact E(2)-invariance through an E(2)-equivariant edge-score network and a categorical continuous-time Markov chain over discrete edge variables. It outperforms previous learning-based state-of-the-art solvers on synthetic TSP (100–10000 nodes) and CVRP (50–2000 customers) while using only 33–50% of the training instances. This work addresses a key limitation of learning-based methods for routing and combinatorial optimization, which previously relied on data augmentation or regularization to approximate E(2)-equivariance. The exact equivariance and discrete diffusion approach could lead to more efficient and robust solvers for logistics, transportation, and network design, benefiting the AI-for-optimization community. EDISCO uses an E(2)-equivariant edge-score network coupled with a categorical continuous-time Markov chain, and exact posterior sampling enables efficient multi-step inference. It also outperforms competing learning-based baselines under spatial distribution shift and CVRP constraint-tightness shift when trained only on uniform synthetic data.

## [TAPDreamer: Transferable Adversarial Patches Attack World Action Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06814) ⭐️ 7.0/10

TAPDreamer constructs a fixed local adversarial patch using only a public encoder that transfers across tasks and action architectures to corrupt world action models without querying the target policy. In closed-loop evaluation, one frozen patch covering about 6.5% of the input reduces FastWAM's success rate from 97.7% to 0.0% across 40 LIBERO tasks and from 90.86% to 0.0% across 50 RoboTwin tasks, while matched random patches retain 81.5% and 79.2% success. This work reveals a critical security vulnerability in world action models, which are increasingly used for general-purpose robotic control, by showing that a single patch optimized on a public encoder can transfer across tasks and architectures without any target-policy queries. It underscores that defenses must secure shared visual encoders, not just downstream action generation, impacting AI security and robotics deployment. The attack leverages the insight that interactions between patch-induced changes in attention weights and value vectors broadcast a nearly identical representation shift far beyond the patch footprint, and this shift remains stable across task observations. Using six frames from one source task, TAPDreamer maximizes the global L1 distance between clean and patched encoder representations; the same patches also reduce success to 1.45% and 1.00% on two DreamWAM configurations and to 10.60% on Motus.

The 27B AutoThink model reaches 73.4 on the public subset of Decision Index 0.3, and RLCD^2 cuts average reasoning length by up to 65% while raising the share of traces that finish within the generation limit by up to 48 percentage points. This work targets a key weakness of reasoning LLMs: they often overthink easy cases and produce overlong traces, so a method that preserves accuracy while cutting reasoning length and improving probability calibration could make deliberative models cheaper and more trustworthy in deployment. The release of open weights and inference code for vLLM and MLX also makes the approach reproducible and usable by practitioners. The Instant models use bidirectional attention in full-attention layers to boost accuracy while keeping single-pass inference, and the AutoThink models only invoke explicit reasoning for uncertain cases; training proceeds in three stages covering shared decision capability, variant specialization, and reasoning supervision plus RLCD^2. RLCD^2 uses a frozen model and proper scoring rules to reward better decision-probability quality and applies a soft penalty to overlong traces, and the paper also introduces DecisionPivot, a programmatically verifiable benchmark built from contrast pairs that differ in a single answer-changing detail.

**Background**: Reasoning LLMs such as chain-of-thought models spend extra computation generating intermediate steps before answering, which improves hard problems but can be wasteful and can produce overlong or unfocused traces. ## [Paper proves success/failure counters are flawed for LLM agent memory safety](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.17544) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.17544v2) formalizes 'reasoning contraction' in LLM agent memory and proves that simple success/failure counters are fundamentally flawed change detectors. Experiments on five LLMs show ExpeL- and ACE-style counters serve 7.0–13.5x more stale answers than certified memories on multi-hop questions, and 35–73x more on code tasks with an exact verifier. This work exposes a hidden safety risk in widely used agent memory systems that rely on counting successes and failures to decide when to trust cached reasoning. It offers a principled alternative that could prevent agents from silently serving wrong answers after facts change, affecting anyone deploying LLM agents with memory. The paper proves that a symmetric counter only notices a partial change after a power of its false-alarm horizon, and an unclipped counter may never notice it. The proposed recipe weighs each memory's failures by its own likelihood ratio, certifies utility against live reasoning, and restarts certification when facts change, with the likelihood-ratio detector as a safety net for unannounced changes; for large edits it also invalidates the memory.

**Background**: LLM agents often reuse past reasoning steps through thought templates, skill libraries, agent memories, and caches—a process the paper calls 'reasoning contraction.' This saves computation but risks stale answers when underlying facts change. The paper shows these counters are poor change detectors and proposes a certified memory approach instead.

## [STOPD: Stochastic Truncation with IPW Speeds Up On-Policy Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21337) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper introduces Stochastic Truncated On-Policy Distillation (STOPD), which randomly truncates student rollouts before generation and corrects the resulting sampling bias using blockwise inverse-probability weighting (IPW). The authors prove that this weighting preserves Vanilla OPD's gradient sum in expectation and derive one-step update-error bounds for SGD, Adam, and Muon. On-policy distillation is computationally expensive due to full rollout generation and per-token teacher feedback, and STOPD reduces generated tokens by 25-48% while maintaining accuracy, achieving 1.3-2.2x training speedups. This makes OPD more practical for LLM training at scale, benefiting ML practitioners working on distillation. At each training step, a stopping position is sampled for each rollout before generation, and the student generates until that position or natural termination; teacher feedback is obtained on every generated token, and blockwise IPW compensates for the lower probability of retaining later tokens while controlling the weights. The method is evaluated across multiple teacher-student model pairs, task domains, and optimizers, though it is a specialized arXiv paper without community discussion.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 22, 04:00

**Background**: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student model by having it generate its own trajectories and then receiving feedback from a teacher model on those trajectories, rather than learning from a fixed dataset. This approach aligns training with the student's own distribution but is costly because it requires generating complete rollouts and computing per-token teacher feedback. Inverse probability weighting (IPW) is a statistical technique that reweights samples to correct for bias when the sampling distribution differs from the target distribution.

## [Training-Free On-Policy Distillation Fuses Specialist Models via Least Squares](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22236) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces a training-free on-policy distillation method that fuses specialist models sharing a base model using only forward passes and a closed-form layer-wise least-squares solution. On Olmo-3-7B, a few GPU-hours of forward computation per specialist produce a generalist that retains most of each specialist's gain across seven mathematics and code benchmarks. This approach eliminates the need for rollouts, teacher passes, and gradient steps per teacher, making model consolidation dramatically cheaper and potentially more accessible for practitioners. It could simplify model merging and efficient specialization, impacting anyone who fine-tunes multiple specialist LLMs from a common base. The layer-wise least-squares solution requires only the second moments of inputs that each specialist receives while reading its own answers, obtained from one forward pass over a few hundred rollouts. The content of rollouts matters more than the solver: removing answers truncated in repetition loops lifts the fused model on AIME25 from task arithmetic's level to the specialist's at matched precision.

## [CCR packs three problems per rollout to cut RLVR token costs by 80%](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22887) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper proposes Concurrent Constraint Reinforcement (CCR), which places three independently verifiable problems into one capped training completion so that correct answers finished before truncation still earn credit. On 4B and 8B math reasoning models, CCR with an 8,000-token window reduced tokens per training step from 975,464 to 174,957 (82.1% savings) and from 793,832 to 165,788 (79.1% savings), respectively, versus single-problem GRPO with a 32k window. Long rollout windows are a major cost driver in RLVR, and naive shortening can erase the correctness signal that group-relative advantages depend on. CCR shows that reward-preserving training structure can deliver large per-step cost reductions while retaining reasoning quality, which matters for anyone training reasoning models at scale. The shared token budget across three problems implicitly encourages shorter useful reasoning without an explicit length penalty, and the authors connect this mechanism to conditional reward- and update-variance analyses. An 8B training trace shows accuracy reward rising alongside shorter completions, with single-problem evaluations providing supporting evidence of retained reasoning quality.

**Background**: RLVR (Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards) trains LLMs using automatically checkable rewards, such as whether a math answer matches the ground truth, instead of learned reward models. The paper proposes MoEvolve, a bidirectional distillation framework that first expands the activation budget of a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model to create a stronger teacher within the model, then reverses distillation to transfer the enhanced capabilities back to the original low-k configuration. It could lead to more efficient post-training pipelines for MoE models, which are increasingly common in both proprietary and open-source LLMs. Naive expansion degrades performance because newly co-activated experts are not optimized to work together; MoEvolve uses a recovery-then-improvement strategy to restore the high-k model before reversing distillation. Notably, the final low-k models often surpass their activation-expanded teachers, and the method retains the original inference-time activation budget.

## [WeAct Adds LoRA Adapter Selection to Agent Action Space](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.26847) ⭐️ 7.0/10

WeAct trains independent capability-specific LoRA adapters over a frozen backbone and adds adapter selection to the agent's action space, using the model's native tool-calling interface for on-demand capability composition. On eight deep-research benchmarks, Qwen3-32B with WeAct improves average accuracy by 6.2% relative to full fine-tuning and by 27.5% relative to the strongest static LoRA-merging method, while using less compute. This approach addresses catastrophic forgetting in long-horizon agents by treating adapter selection as an internal action, enabling modular continual adaptation without retraining the backbone. It could benefit developers building agents that must handle heterogeneous tasks over extended trajectories, offering a parameter-efficient alternative to joint training or static adapter merging. WeAct supports modular continual adaptation by adding a new code computation adapter and updating an existing writing adapter while leaving the backbone and other adapters unchanged. The method leverages the model's native tool-calling interface, and the reported gains are on Qwen3-32B across eight deep-research benchmarks.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 22, 04:00

**Background**: LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) is a parameter-efficient fine-tuning technique that adds small trainable matrices to selected layers while keeping the original model weights frozen, drastically reducing the number of trainable parameters. Catastrophic forgetting is the tendency of neural networks to abruptly forget previously learned information when trained on new data, which is a major challenge for continual learning. Long-horizon agents must learn multiple capabilities from interleaved trajectories, and updating shared parameters can degrade earlier skills.

langchain-core 1.7.0 now emits `tool-call-delta` slices for streamed tool-call arguments instead of `block-delta` snapshots of the arguments so far. This is a breaking change for developers who consume raw stream events and read `block-delta` args mid-stream. Streaming allows tokens or tool-call arguments to be delivered incrementally as they are generated, which is useful for real-time user interfaces. Previously, streamed tool-call arguments were emitted as `block-delta` events that contained a snapshot of all arguments received so far; the new `tool-call-delta` events instead provide only the newly generated slice, requiring consumers to accumulate the pieces themselves.

## [LightCRS: Lightweight Multi-Domain Conversational Recommendation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.26948) ⭐️ 6.0/10

LightCRS introduces a lightweight, query-conditioned cross-attention framework that unifies multi-domain multimodal conversational recommendation using frozen encoders and a compact shared 5.3M-parameter module. It also constructs MM-R2A-25, a 25-domain benchmark pairing Reddit conversations with Amazon product listings, and achieves state-of-the-art HR@1, NDCG@5, and MRR while reducing per-query latency by 266 times. This work addresses the scalability dilemma in deploying vision-language models for conversational recommendation across many product domains, where separate models scale cost linearly and naive merging degrades accuracy. By sharing parameters across domains and using frozen encoders, LightCRS offers a practical path to efficient multi-domain deployment, potentially benefiting e-commerce platforms and conversational AI systems. LightCRS precomputes multimodal product representations offline with frozen encoders, then online fuses evidence via query-conditioned cross-attention with parameters shared across all domains, and compares candidates jointly with an inter-candidate Transformer. Joint multi-domain training improves HR@1 by 15.2% over separately trained single-domain models, and the approach achieves a 35.4% HR@1 improvement over the strongest baseline.

## [M-Plan: Closed-Loop Multi-Agent Framework with Memory Arrangement for LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.27032) ⭐️ 6.0/10

Researchers propose M-Plan, a closed-loop multi-agent system framework that integrates long-term and short-term memory to improve LLM agents on long-horizon tasks. It combines global-local and past-current guidance, providing task-specific milestones and insights, and only gives local hints when the agent is confused; after task completion, relevant information is optimized or reorganized before being stored in long-term memory. Long-horizon tasks remain a major weakness for LLM agents, and existing memory-augmented multi-agent systems either retrieve memories without task adaptation or lack memory tailored to task-specific guidance. M-Plan's plug-and-play design and reported gains on ALFWorld, Webshop, and PDDL suggest a practical way to make agents more reliable in multi-turn, real-world environments. The framework's short-term memory is formed by the generation and use of guidance during execution, while long-term memory stores reorganized task information for future retrieval. Experiments across diverse models on ALFWorld, Webshop, and PDDL show improvements in both accuracy and efficiency over multiple baselines, though the abstract is truncated and no independent validation or code release is mentioned.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 22, 04:00

**Background**: LLM-based agents handle single-turn tasks well but struggle with long-horizon tasks that require dozens to hundreds of interleaved reasoning steps, partly because LLMs have difficulty processing long contexts. Multi-agent systems with long-term memory attempt to address this, but often rely on direct knowledge retrieval or summarization without adapting memories to the current task, and retrieved memories may contain historical noise. M-Plan aims to combine task-specific guidance with a memory pipeline that cleans and reorganizes information before storage.

The framework uses logical entropy to construct answering trajectories where each step is associated with a measurable entropy reduction, and experiments show that higher entropy correlates with more false positives, validating entropy as a monotonic selector for correct reasoning paths. A new arXiv paper proposes a control variate built from a learned classifier of feeder outages, trained on cheap observable features like temperature and load forecasts, to reduce the number of expensive grid simulator runs needed for rare-event Monte Carlo estimation. The authors prove that variance reduction is an explicit function of the classifier's recall and false-positive rate, and show that a Gaussian load proxy loses effectiveness as outages become rarer while a learner with non-vanishing precision keeps removing a fixed fraction of variance. This work addresses a practical bottleneck in power system planning: estimating very small outage probabilities with plain Monte Carlo requires a prohibitive number of simulator runs. By reducing variance with a cheap learned classifier, the method could help planners design more reliable distribution grids against rare EV-induced overloads, as demonstrated in a case study of Surabaya, Indonesia, where it reduced city-wide blackout days by a third compared with Monte Carlo at the same simulation budget. Numerical experiments across three orders of magnitude of outage probability show that even a weak single-feature learner removes a quarter of the variance, while a boosted-tree learner removes about 60%. In the Surabaya feeder network, the Gaussian load model leaves every feeder three to seven times the one-day-in-ten-years blackout target, and planning with the learned CV and a 95% confidence limit reduces blackout days by a third.

By comparing the representations of thirty-five existing LLM-based research agents with the RPG, the authors find that each agent is an incomplete RPG, as none keeps the changed state, the evidence that changed it, and the reasoning connecting them as one evolving record. The RPG is grounded in authentic trajectories whose steps are justified by authors in annotations and papers, and it enables agents to predict the next research state instead of a complete idea, evaluate ideas as trajectories instead of final texts, and use authentic trajectories as training data. In Study A (13 clinical queries over 20 patient records), the Temporal-15 configuration achieved a milestone slot recall of 0.538 versus 0.388 for the Global-50 baseline, though it also retrieved far more evidence (496 versus 50 indexed units per query). This work highlights a key failure mode in clinical retrieval: similarity-based ranking over-represents repeated diagnoses and misses one-time pivotal events like recurrence or therapy changes. It could influence how clinical NLP and IR systems are designed for longitudinal electronic health records, especially under fixed evidence budgets. The reported recall gain cannot be attributed to allocation alone because the Temporal-15 configuration retrieves roughly ten times more evidence per query. When evidence is held fixed, removing prompted precedence rules raises schema-order reversals from 0.010 to 0.080, and a five-patient single-query pilot finds that wider temporal coverage does not reliably yield more dated milestones; without expert reference timelines, the measurements describe retrieval behavior rather than clinical accuracy.

**Background**: Electronic health records are written to support care rather than retrieval, so the same primary diagnosis is often restated across years of notes while pivotal events such as recurrence or a change in therapy may appear only once. This creates temporal redundancy: a retriever that ranks passages by similarity to the query keeps returning repeated material and can miss the transitions that shape a patient's course. The paper frames longitudinal clinical retrieval as allocating a limited evidence budget across time and separates the task into temporal evidence allocation, candidate reconstruction, and clinical validation.

## [EASformer disentangles environment, action, and state for industrial generative ranking](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.27691) ⭐️ 6.0/10

EASformer introduces an Environment-Action-State disentangled Transformer architecture that explicitly aligns historical and non-sequential tokens in a shared context environment space while separating user actions from candidate-specific context. On an offline benchmark from a real-world industrial app marketplace it achieves an AUC of 0.89411 (0.88% relative gain over the deployed baseline), and online A/B tests show relative eCPM lifts of 1.26% and 3.94% across two ranking scenarios. The paper addresses a real semantic asymmetry in generative recommendation: query-key dot products between historical and candidate-side representations can compare different semantic objects, limiting cross-token interaction. Its disentangled design and Cloze-style self-supervised objective offer a practical path for industrial ranking systems that tokenize long behavior sequences and heterogeneous features, though the gains are incremental and specific to app-marketplace ranking. EASformer builds an explicitly aligned context environment space shared by historical and non-sequence tokens, enabling complementary historical action retrieval and state-conditioned action prediction. The disentangled design also supports a Cloze-style self-supervised objective that masks historical actions and reuses the candidate prediction pathway, with evaluation limited to one industrial app marketplace and two online scenarios.

Disentangled representation learning aims to separate underlying factors in observed data, and EASformer applies this idea to distinguish environment context, observed user actions, and candidate state in industrial ranking.

## [Fine-tuning objectives shape layer-wise representations in LLM hallucination detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.27711) ⭐️ 6.0/10

A new arXiv paper analyzes how classifier-head fine-tuning (cls) versus sequence-to-sequence fine-tuning (s2s) affects layer-wise representations in LLM hallucination detection, finding that cls yields more discriminative and linearly decodable features. The study also identifies an 'InfoWindow' in upper-middle layers where task information emerges, and shows that truncating 31% of the network leaves accuracy unchanged while cutting latency by 1.4x on Qwen3-4B and 8B. This work provides a mechanistic understanding of why certain fine-tuning objectives lead to better hallucination detection, which could guide more efficient task-specific LLM design. The finding that a large fraction of upper layers can be removed without accuracy loss has practical implications for reducing inference cost in detection systems. The cls paradigm learns a task-specific discriminative direction that creates a clear two-cluster geometry, while s2s relies on the pretrained language-modeling head and leaves hidden states closer to the backbone. The layer truncation fraction was fixed before analyzing target models and transferred to Llama-3.2-3B and Mistral-7B-v0.3, with the same layer structure reappearing on QNLI and SST-2.

A controlled evaluation on a HighwayEnv testbed shows that reported gains from experience memory in closed-loop LLM driving agents are largely attributable to the specific warmup pool draw and prompt token effects, not memory itself. The study finds that the reported pool is the best of ten for retrieval memories, which beat No-Memory in only one pool, and that no retrieval design exceeds a token-matched filler baseline. This work challenges the claimed benefits of experience memory in LLM-based driving agents, highlighting the need for rigorous controls such as resampled warmup pools and token-matched fillers in future evaluations. It affects researchers and practitioners developing memory-augmented LLM agents for autonomous driving and other sequential decision-making domains. The evaluation uses ten disjoint warmup pools, token-matched irrelevant-filler controls, oracle-certified diagnostics, and audited baseline ports on a 1Hz HighwayEnv testbed with gpt-4o-mini. Findings include that a single 15-token caution instruction reaches the collision-only merge ceiling and that baseline port quality can silently invert conclusions.

LatBridge introduces a shared Bridge and reusable low-rank interfaces to enable stable model replacement in latent-communication multi-agent systems without retraining frozen models. After replacement, it reuses unchanged interfaces, selects matching low-rank interfaces, and trains only missing ones while keeping all models frozen. This addresses a key limitation of existing latent-communication methods, which assume fixed model combinations and fail when agents are swapped. Experiments across eight small-model configurations show mean basic-mode accuracies of 14.8% on MATH and 27.3% on ALFWorld next-action prediction, with analyses examining factors supporting task accuracy and communication efficiency.

## [SAPD: Offline Policy Distillation for LLM Agents Without Environment Interaction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.27847) ⭐️ 6.0/10

A new arXiv preprint (2610.27847) introduces Step-Advantage Policy Distillation (SAPD), a method that trains LLM agents from offline trajectories by decomposing multi-turn trajectories into individual decision contexts for on-policy distillation and using relative step-advantage signals to stabilize training. The approach requires neither new environment observations nor additional multi-turn interactions, and experiments on ALFWorld, WebShop, and Search-based QA show improved performance, reduced catastrophic forgetting versus SFT, and at least 4.7× faster per training step than online OPD. Scaling LLM agent training is bottlenecked by the cost of building and maintaining executable environments, so a method that reuses existing offline trajectories without live interaction could substantially lower the barrier to agent post-training. By avoiding both the catastrophic forgetting of SFT and the real-time cost of online RL, SAPD points toward a more practical middle ground for agent improvement. SAPD performs on-policy distillation in which the student generates responses conditioned on recorded histories, and it introduces relative step-advantage signals to stabilize training; the abstract reports gains across different teacher configurations and at least 4.7× faster per training step than online OPD. The work is an early preprint with code promised soon, and the abstract is truncated, so full empirical validation is not yet available.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 22, 04:00

**Background**: LLM agents are typically trained either by supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on demonstration trajectories, which can cause catastrophic forgetting of general capabilities, or by online reinforcement learning, which requires costly real-time interaction with executable environments. On-policy distillation (OPD) instead has the student model generate its own sequences and a teacher provide feedback on them, turning distillation into an iterative correction process. SAPD extends this idea to the offline setting by reusing recorded multi-turn trajectories as decision contexts, aiming to get OPD-like benefits without environment access.

## [Staged Training of Multimodal Models Shows Non-Additive Phase Effects](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.27904) ⭐️ 6.0/10

A new arXiv paper tracks an 8.4B-parameter multimodal foundation model through three staged post-training phases on Japanese financial documents and finds that the phases interact non-additively. Specifically, math-only distillation overwrites earlier financial knowledge even as procedural math skill survives, and the domain phase repairs more than it installs. This work challenges the common assumption that multi-stage post-training pipelines yield additive improvements, showing instead that per-phase contributions are not decomposable and that the best checkpoint is task-dependent. Practitioners designing continual or staged training schedules may need to rethink checkpoint retention and phase ordering rather than simply adding more stages. The study evaluates the model on five text-input benchmarks and includes a skip-phase ablation, which is best for domain knowledge but forfeits numerical-reasoning gains. The findings are based on a single 8.4B model in a narrow domain (Japanese financial documents), limiting broader generalization.

## [TrajEvolve: Trajectory Evolution with Hindsight Credit Assignment for LLM RL](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28060) ⭐️ 6.0/10

TrajEvolve introduces a trajectory evolution paradigm that refines low-quality steps in historical trajectories to generate 'evolutionary trajectories', exposing the policy to high-quality compositions rarely sampled within training budgets. It also reformulates step-level credit assignment as a binary classification task—whether each step is necessary—with labels obtained via counterfactual verification, and experiments on two datasets show superiority over baselines. This work addresses two key bottlenecks in applying RL to long-horizon LLM reasoning: sparse successful trajectories and indiscriminate credit assignment from sparse final rewards. If validated, it could improve sample efficiency and reduce redundant step generation in RL training for complex reasoning tasks. TrajEvolve extends the GRPO algorithm by periodically invoking a trained discriminator to assess step-level credit for newly collected trajectories, and the binary classification simplification reduces learning difficulty while enabling precise identification of redundant steps through counterfactual verification. The work is an early-stage arXiv preprint with experiments on only two datasets and no community discussion yet.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 22, 04:00

**Background**: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards has become a standard approach for improving LLM reasoning, but long-horizon tasks make it hard to obtain enough successful trajectories and to assign credit to individual steps when only a sparse final reward is available. Hindsight credit assignment is a technique that re-evaluates past actions using information about what actually happened later, and GRPO is a policy optimization algorithm that estimates advantages from groups of sampled outputs. TrajEvolve combines these ideas by evolving trajectories and turning step-level credit assignment into a binary classification problem.

## [Conditional Information Bottleneck Boosts Robustness of Spiking Neural Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28110) ⭐️ 6.0/10

The paper proposes SCIB, a conditional information bottleneck objective for spiking neural networks (SNNs) that replaces the standard mutual information compression term I(X;S) with the conditional mutual information I(X;S|Y) and introduces a learnable class-conditional prior. Experiments on Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100 show improved robustness against environmental noise, neuromorphic hardware noise, and adversarial attacks, along with a 24.9% reduction in SynOps-based single-sample inference energy compared to an unconstrained SNN baseline. SNNs are promising for low-power neuromorphic computing but remain vulnerable to perturbations and noise, limiting real-world deployment. SCIB offers a simple, principled training objective that improves robustness without adversarial training and even reduces energy consumption, which could accelerate the adoption of SNNs in edge and neuromorphic hardware. SCIB derives a tractable variational upper bound for the conditional mutual information and uses a learnable class-conditional prior instead of a label-agnostic isotropic Gaussian prior, encouraging class-structured representations. The method improves adversarial accuracy under evaluated attacks without adversarial training, but the evaluation is limited to three image datasets and specific noise models.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 22, 04:00

**Background**: Spiking neural networks are brain-inspired networks that process information using discrete spikes, offering event-driven processing and spatiotemporal sparsity for low-power neuromorphic computing. The information bottleneck principle is an information-theoretic framework that learns compressed representations preserving task-relevant information, typically by minimizing mutual information I(X;S) between input X and representation S while maximizing I(S;Y) with label Y. Conditional information bottleneck extends this by conditioning on Y, compressing information not relevant to the label.

## [Interruption-Aware Recurrent RL Improves UAS Navigation Safety After Overrides](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28121) ⭐️ 6.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.28121) shows that temporary overrides by remote pilots or safety systems degrade recurrent reinforcement learning policies for UAS navigation, making task variables less decodable from hidden states and increasing post-interruption collision risk. The authors propose three interruption-aware architectures that condition recurrent processing on interruption context, with the strongest reducing post-interruption collisions by 74% and interruption-induced mission failures by 69% compared to a standard recurrent baseline. This research addresses a critical safety gap in autonomous UAS operations: ensuring safe handback of control after human or automated overrides. As recurrent RL policies become more common for navigation under partial observability, understanding and mitigating interruption effects is essential for certification and real-world deployment in shared airspace. The paper identifies an action-observation feedback loop where changed actions after handback alter the flight path and subsequent recurrent updates, prolonging degradation. The three architectures use separate feature streams, dedicated interruption memory, or gated environmental features, and all preserve more decodable task information than a standard recurrent policy without degrading interruption-free performance.

The paper introduces G-JEPA, a latent world model that incorporates a shared causal temporal module to aggregate temporal context for physical grounding and couples it with prior-guided action planning. ## [AnomalyAgent: VLM-Guided Ensemble Fusion for Visual Anomaly Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28560) ⭐️ 6.0/10

AnomalyAgent introduces a post-training fusion framework that aligns heterogeneous scores and anomaly maps from multiple pretrained detectors and treats fusion as a finite action-selection problem. A constrained vision-language model inspects high-conflict samples and selects valid score and map actions to produce the final prediction. This work addresses a key limitation of fixed-rule ensembles when pretrained detectors disagree, potentially improving robustness in visual anomaly detection where anomalous samples are scarce. It demonstrates how vision-language models can be used as adaptive fusion agents, which could influence future ensemble design in industrial inspection and medical imaging. The framework defines two action types: score actions (consensus, robust aggregation, detector weighting, score-map consistency) and map actions (consensus, detector weighting, geometric aggregation, disagreement correction). Evaluated on MVTec AD and VisA as primary benchmarks plus seven additional public benchmarks and Real-IAD, it achieves the best mean image AUROC and pixel AP among compared fusion methods.

The core module, Uncertainty-Gated Update (UG-Update), estimates reliability via intra-class dispersion and selectively gates residual gradient updates, while an Uncertainty-Based Pseudo Label Filter (UB-Filter) enforces learning from high-confidence signals. UGA estimates episodic reliability using intra-class dispersion over merged support and pseudo-labeled novel supervision, and gates residual gradient updates accordingly. The method is evaluated on ScanNet200 and ScanNet++ under 1-shot and 5-shot settings, showing consistent improvements over prior methods.

## [CA-MOPD: Capability-Aware Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.26950) ⭐️ 6.0/10

The paper introduces CA-MOPD, a multi-teacher on-policy distillation method that first merges reinforcement-learning specialists into a strong student initialization, then uses verifier-estimated teacher-student capability gaps to adjust per-domain distillation strength instead of relying on behavioral discrepancy. Across six benchmarks spanning mathematics, code generation, and instruction following, CA-MOPD achieves an average score of 32.22, outperforming naive MOPD, Open-MOPD, and the merged initialization by 0.86, 0.83, and 0.74 points, respectively. This work addresses a key inefficiency in multi-teacher distillation: behavioral mismatch does not necessarily imply a remaining capability deficit, so discrepancy-based allocation can over-supervise domains where the student already matches or exceeds the teacher. By allocating supervision based on estimated capability gaps, CA-MOPD offers a more principled way to integrate domain specialists, which could improve the efficiency and effectiveness of post-training pipelines for large language models. CA-MOPD decreases supervision as capability gaps close and increases it when estimated student capability regresses, while dense token-level guidance remains provided by the teachers. Controlled comparisons under matched training budgets further support the benefits of merged initialization and capability-gap guidance.

**Background**: Knowledge distillation trains a smaller student model to reproduce the behavior of larger teacher models, and on-policy distillation specifically uses the student's own rollouts for training. Multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) extends this to combine multiple domain-specialized reinforcement-learning teachers into a single student, but deciding how strongly each teacher should supervise each domain remains an open problem. The paper introduces BMO, a boundary-aware model obfuscation method that decomposes model parameters into boundary-position and boundary-curvature components using null-space constraints, then injects noise into the curvature component to diversify decision boundaries across deployed models. Evaluated on four widely-deployed on-device models against four major adversarial attack types, BMO achieves an average defense success rate of 68.68%, compared to 22.32% for the strongest baseline, while maintaining comparable benign accuracy. BMO offers a practical defense that diversifies decision boundaries without sacrificing accuracy, addressing a critical security gap in on-device machine learning. BMO leverages the finding that model robustness is primarily influenced by decision-boundary curvature, and it instantiates differentiated models by injecting noise into the curvature component while preserving benign accuracy. The abstract is truncated, so full details on the null-space decomposition and noise injection mechanism are not available in the provided content.

The von Mises-Fisher distribution is a probability distribution on the unit hypersphere, often used in directional statistics, and its kernel can smooth similarity computations to avoid over-concentration. ## [Trail-Weighted Pruning Scores for Approximate Bayesian Network Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.27366) ⭐️ 6.0/10

The paper introduces trail-weighted pruning of evidence for Bayesian-network prediction, where a traversal scores each active trail by the product of its edge strengths and drops evidence below a threshold. It proves an error bound for collider-free networks (chains and forks) over binary variables and shows in simulations on random trees that thresholding trail scores yields 1.4 to 13 times lower error than random pruning of the same size. This work provides a theoretically grounded pruning criterion for approximate inference in Bayesian networks, which could help reduce computation in probabilistic graphical models when exact inference is expensive. It also offers insights into when local trail scores are reliable, though the lack of speedup in real networks limits immediate practical impact. The proven bound holds only when each dropped trail lies in its own branch of the outcome node and fails when dropped trails share a branch; for general networks with colliders and loops, the score is used as an unproven heuristic. On seven bnlearn networks, keeping the top half of evidence by trail score beat random pruning but was not clearly better than mutual-information ranking, and scoring cost more than the inference it saved on six of seven networks, so no speedup was observed.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 22, 04:00

**Background**: Bayesian networks are probabilistic graphical models that represent conditional dependencies among variables via a directed acyclic graph, and inference in them can be computationally expensive. In such graphs, paths between variables are classified into patterns like chains, forks, and colliders, which determine whether evidence propagates (active trails) or is blocked. Approximate inference methods often prune less relevant evidence to speed up prediction, but pruning without guarantees can introduce large errors.

This arXiv paper proposes a model inversion attack using Deep Convolutional Generative Adversarial Networks (DCGANs) on federated learning systems for large-scale medical imaging, and evaluates client-side differential privacy as a defense. Experiments on the Brain MRI ND-5 dataset show that the attack can reconstruct semantically meaningful synthetic images, while differential privacy reduces attack success at the cost of accuracy, which personalized federated learning helps mitigate. The work highlights that federated learning alone does not guarantee privacy for sensitive medical data, and that attackers can exploit shared model updates to reconstruct training images. It provides a model-agnostic attack-and-defense framework that can inform the design of privacy-preserving federated learning systems in healthcare and other regulated domains. CVG-SGM introduces a transfer-maintain-read memory mechanism that stores target-carrier bindings to recover object identities when an object disappears inside an opaque carrier and reappears as a fresh detection. In controlled one-identity-per-carrier settings, it achieves 1.000 re-link accuracy versus 0.570 for no-memory and parameter-matched no-write controls, and correctly re-links 36/36 held-out detections on real RGB-D/SAM2 feature-level episodes. The method uses geometry-weighted cross-node interaction to transfer target evidence into carrier states, a shared per-node GRU to maintain it during transport, and a two-time readout combining stored carrier-identity compatibility with current detection-carrier geometry. It generalizes to scene-disjoint unseen longer gaps, but remains limited by shared-carrier identity ambiguity and does not provide end-to-end raw-video re-identification.

## [AnchorRM enables parallel intra-batch state reconstruction for temporal GNNs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.27558) ⭐️ 6.0/10

AnchorRM introduces an anchor-based residual memory mechanism that reconstructs event-specific intra-batch node states in memory-based temporal graph neural networks without sequential recurrent updates. By treating the last committed memory as a fixed anchor and predicting residuals from causal history, it achieves an average 6.16x training speedup (up to 10.05x) and 28.67x batch scaling (up to 40x) across four datasets and three backbones. This work addresses a fundamental inefficiency in memory-based temporal graph learning: stale memory during temporal mini-batching, which worsens with larger batch sizes. By enabling parallel reconstruction while preserving temporal causality, AnchorRM could significantly improve the scalability and training efficiency of TGNs for large-scale dynamic graph applications. The reconstructed states are computed in parallel because each event-specific residual depends only on the fixed anchor and its causal history, not on previously reconstructed states. Experiments show competitive predictive performance, but the approach is evaluated on four temporal graph datasets and three memory-based backbones, so generalization to other architectures remains to be tested.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 22, 04:00

**Background**: Memory-based temporal graph neural networks (TGNs) maintain a memory vector for each node that summarizes its interaction history and is updated recurrently as events occur. Temporal mini-batching groups events into batches for efficient training, but when a node appears multiple times in a batch, later events use the stale pre-batch memory because updates are not committed until the batch ends. This creates a trade-off between computational efficiency and temporal fidelity, which becomes more severe with larger batches.

## [Anytime-Valid Runtime Monitoring of Learned Barrier Certificates](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.27726) ⭐️ 6.0/10

The paper introduces an anytime-valid runtime monitor that audits learned barrier certificates for stochastic systems by formulating the conditional barrier-drift condition as an episode-wise sequential hypothesis test. Observed barrier increments are transformed into a nonnegative test supermartingale, yielding finite-sample false-alarm control under arbitrary stopping times, and a deterministic temporal shaping of the monitoring boundary makes the monitor more conservative early in a prescribed deployment horizon. This work addresses the gap between offline-certified safety and deployment-time validity, offering a statistically rigorous way to detect when a learned barrier certificate no longer holds as dynamics shift. It could benefit safety-critical applications of stochastic systems where certificates are learned from data and may degrade in the field. The monitor detects loss of statistical support for the deployed barrier condition but does not guarantee detection before unsafe entry or safety of a subsequent intervention; it is designed to flag statistical evidence of inconsistency rather than predict unsafe entry. Empirical evaluation covers alarm behavior under both valid and invalid certificates, with code and data available on GitHub.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 22, 04:00

**Background**: Barrier certificates are functions of state used to formally verify that a stochastic system remains within a safe region, and learned barrier certificates are trained from data to provide such guarantees. However, their validity can deteriorate when deployment dynamics differ from training, motivating runtime monitoring. Anytime-valid sequential tests, built on test supermartingales, allow continuous monitoring of streaming data with false-alarm guarantees that hold regardless of when one stops.

Researchers propose VISH (Viterbi-guided Selection of Hotwords), a training-free, plug-and-play framework that verifies candidate hotwords directly over frame-level CTC posteriors, with M-VISH scaling large-list verification via frame-synchronous shared-prefix Viterbi search and bounded top-K pruning, and Bi-MVISH adding backward evidence. The method freezes a shared BEATs audio transformer and isolates each new domain as a low-rank expert, avoiding parameter interference; at inference, the router retrieves the top-two candidate experts and fuses domain-routing posteriors with classification confidence, weighted by estimated ambiguity. ## [BAIT benchmark tests LLMs' ability to spot cognitive bias triggers in news](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28092) ⭐️ 6.0/10

Researchers introduced BAIT (Bias Annotation In Text), a benchmark that pairs a schema of nine cognitive bias triggers with 50 English news articles annotated at the article and span levels by trained annotators and adjudicated into a gold standard. They benchmarked six frontier LLMs zero-shot and with three or ten in-context examples on two tasks: detecting which triggers a text contains and locating the spans that carry them. As LLMs increasingly mediate how people encounter news—summarizing, ranking, and answering questions over it—their ability to recognize manipulative language is critical for media literacy and LLM safety. The finding that models respond to surface cues rather than the mechanisms that make a passage manipulative suggests current LLMs may not reliably flag biased content. The dataset is small (50 articles), and while models approach human agreement on which triggers an article contains, they rarely recover the full set of triggers and reach less than half of human agreement in locating the passages that carry them. Models also over-predict triggers with easy surface cues, and most passages they mark for these triggers are not actual triggers but often contain the trigger's surface cue far more than random text.

## [TEPCA co-aligns LLM evidence and parameters for temporal knowledge graph reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28176) ⭐️ 6.0/10

The paper introduces TEPCA, a framework that aligns LLM reasoning with temporal knowledge graphs at both the evidence level (via time-constrained Dynamic Relevance-Guided Path pruning and mutual-information-based pruning) and the parameter level (via Dynamic-Gated LoRA, a timestamp-conditioned low-rank adaptation). Experiments on two TKG benchmarks show state-of-the-art performance, and DG-LoRA is further validated on eight commonsense QA datasets. LLMs often fail at temporally grounded reasoning because their static parametric memory conflicts with evolving real-world facts; TEPCA offers a dual-level alignment approach that could improve retrieval-augmented generation and parameter-efficient fine-tuning for time-sensitive applications. This matters for anyone building LLM systems that must reason over changing knowledge, such as dynamic QA, event forecasting, and agent memory. TEPCA combines DRGP pruning to preserve globally coherent temporal paths with MI-based pruning to retain query-informative local facts under temporal constraints, while DG-LoRA dynamically modulates the effective adaptation subspace based on temporal context. The approach is evaluated on two TKG benchmarks and DG-LoRA alone on eight commonsense QA datasets, demonstrating scalability across LLM backbones and interpretability.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 22, 04:00

**Background**: Temporal knowledge graphs (TKGs) extend standard knowledge graphs by attaching timestamps to facts, enabling reasoning about how entities and relations evolve over time. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) enhances LLMs by fetching external evidence, but typically ignores temporal validity, while parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) adapts LLMs with few trainable parameters but often uses fixed, input-agnostic updates. TEPCA addresses both limitations by making retrieval and adaptation time-aware.

## [CALM: Offline-Calibrated Layer-Head Token Merging for Video KV-Cache Compression](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28192) ⭐️ 6.0/10

The paper introduces CALM (Calibrated Allocation for Layer-Head Merging), which observes that different attention layers and heads in autoregressive video models have distinct but prompt-consistent sensitivities to token merging, and uses offline calibration of layer-head merging ratios to improve online KV-cache compression. Instead of a uniform merging ratio, CALM builds a fixed layer-head risk map offline using attention-output error as a proxy for end-to-end video quality, then applies dynamic programming at inference to allocate merging ratios under a given cache budget. KV-cache memory is a major bottleneck for long-horizon autoregressive video generation, and CALM shows that a lightweight offline calibration can consistently beat uniform token merging across three different models, reducing LPIPS by about 21% at the same memory budget. This suggests that per-layer, per-head allocation policies are a practical, low-overhead path to more efficient video generation without retraining. Exhaustively evaluating all layer-head allocations is prohibitively expensive, so CALM relies on the empirical finding that attention-output error strongly correlates with end-to-end video quality and uses it as a lightweight risk proxy. The risk map is computed once offline, and at inference a dynamic programming solver picks the best merging-ratio allocation for the available cache budget; results are reported on three autoregressive video models with higher video-quality scores than uniform merging.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 22, 04:00

**Background**: Autoregressive video generation models produce frames sequentially and keep a growing key-value (KV) cache of past tokens to attend to, which quickly becomes a memory bottleneck for long videos. Token merging reduces this cost by clustering temporally redundant tokens and keeping only a few representatives, but prior methods apply the same merging ratio to every attention layer and head. CALM builds on the observation that layers and heads play different functional roles and thus tolerate different amounts of merging, an idea also explored in concurrent KV-compression work for autoregressive video diffusion.

## [Adaptive Pullback OPD Reweights Supervision at Penalty Jumps](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28194) ⭐️ 6.0/10

The paper identifies abrupt 'penalty jumps' in on-policy distillation (OPD), where average token penalties rise while teacher confidence drops, and proposes Adaptive Pullback OPD (AP-OPD) to reweight supervision at these jumps. AP-OPD uses the preceding block as a local reference to uniformly scale supervision coefficients in the following block so that its weighted average penalty matches the preceding block's original mean, eliminating the need for an additional strength constant. This work offers a diagnostic (penalty-confidence tension) and a principled method to improve on-policy distillation, which is increasingly used to transfer capabilities from large teacher models to smaller deployable students. AP-OPD improves performance on mathematical reasoning and code generation, suggesting practical benefits for LLM training pipelines. The diagnostic compares consecutive blocks of tokens within the same response to detect penalty jumps that persist on held-out tokens, and shows that boundaries into high-penalty blocks do not exhibit comparable confidence changes. AP-OPD's scaling factor is determined solely by the preceding block's mean penalty, avoiding an extra hyperparameter, though the method's reliance on block-level statistics may introduce sensitivity to block size.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 22, 04:00

**Background**: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student model on its own generated responses, using token-level log-ratios between student and teacher distributions as supervision signals. A positive log-ratio penalizes tokens where the student assigns higher probability than the teacher, but the raw value does not distinguish sustained high penalties from abrupt increases. This paper analyzes local changes in penalties to identify meaningful jumps and proposes a reweighting scheme to stabilize training.

The authors introduce JAXbounce, a fully differentiable and parallelizable continuous-control Pong-like benchmark in JAX for evaluating active inference agents beyond discrete, low-dimensional environments. They validate it with over 10,000 simulations comparing a deterministic baseline, a state-based active inference agent using an Unscented Kalman Filter and expected free energy planning, and a pixel-based agent with a pretrained neural network encoder across three difficulty levels and eight noise conditions. This benchmark fills a genuine gap by extending active inference evaluation to continuous state spaces and stochastic dynamics, which are more representative of real-world control problems. It provides a reproducible platform that could standardize comparisons and accelerate research in the active inference and JAX communities. JAXbounce offers flexible observation models (state vector or pixel grid) and a rich family of noise models, and its full differentiability and parallelizability in JAX enable efficient large-scale experimentation. The study characterizes how performance scales with planning horizon, observation modality, and knowledge of the noise process, showing preference-oriented behavior even under increasing uncertainty.

TPO introduces a tri-level distributionally robust learning framework that jointly models group-level, prompt-level, and preference-level distribution shifts in Direct Preference Optimization (DPO). By using a hierarchically structured rectangular ambiguity set instantiated with Wasserstein distance, it derives a tractable objective combining a closed-form preference-level margin penalty, prompt-level adversarial embedding perturbation, and worst-case group reweighting, each with an independent radius. This work addresses a critical gap in robust DPO by explicitly modeling the hierarchical structure of out-of-distribution preference shifts, which is essential for safe LLM deployment in diverse real-world scenarios. It could lead to more reliable alignment methods that generalize better to unseen user groups, prompts, and preference patterns. The framework provides finite-sample convergence guarantees and empirical validation against existing robust DPO methods. However, as an arXiv preprint, it has not yet undergone peer review, and its practical impact depends on further validation and adoption.

## [Gated Prototype Transfer Boosts Zero-Support Class Recall in Medical VLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28350) ⭐️ 6.0/10

The paper introduces Gated Knowledge-Guided Prototype Transfer (GProtoT), a pre-repulsion module that transfers visual residuals from supported classes to zero-support classes using VLM similarity and an ontology-based clinical distance. In 50 paired one-shot trials on MESSIDOR with FLAIR features, GProtoT improved missing-class recall by 5.23 points over the SS-Text+ baseline while reducing negative-transfer frequency from 46-48% to 2%. This work addresses a critical gap in few-shot medical imaging where low-prevalence classes lack any labeled support, enabling safer adaptation of vision-language models in clinical settings with incomplete supervision. The training-free, gradient-free approach offers a low-compute path toward accountable AI deployment in healthcare. GProtoT requires no gradients, validation data, or additional model inference, but it incurs a trade-off: supported-class recall drops by 1.20 percentage points and top-1 accuracy by 0.45 percentage points. The evidence gate scales transfer based on semantic relevance and residual agreement to limit unsupported extrapolation.

## [RayCo4D: Ray-Conditioned Continuous Motion Model for Monocular 4D Reconstruction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28351) ⭐️ 6.0/10

RayCo4D introduces a ray-conditioned continuous motion model that separates visual measurements from latent 3D motion states, using SE(3) nodes with a white-noise-on-acceleration prior to reconstruct dynamic 3D scenes from monocular video. The method associates each track with a reference-time 3D query constrained to its camera ray and constrains shared latent motion nodes through local many-to-many associations. This work addresses the challenge of integrating fragmented temporal observations from long-range tracks into a shared continuous motion representation, which could improve structural and temporal consistency in monocular 4D reconstruction under rapid motion and incomplete tracks. It represents a meaningful incremental contribution to the dynamic scene reconstruction community. Each motion node maintains an SE(3) pose and body-frame velocity at sparse support times, and the inferred shared motion is transferred to Gaussian primitives via dual-quaternion blending, while reference-anchored local SE(3) residuals capture fine-scale non-rigid deformation. Experiments show competitive novel-view synthesis quality and support for continuous-time rendering.
